title: Good to Great
subtitle: Why Some Companies Make the Leap and Others Don't
author: Jim Collins
why_it_matters: It set the template for evidence-driven business writing: find companies that beat the market for fifteen years, match them against near-identical rivals, and ask what differed. The method has been attacked hard since, but the questions it forced into boardrooms are still the right ones.

crux.headline: Greatness is a discipline, not a burst of brilliance
crux.body: Sustained outperformance did not come from a charismatic saviour, a bold acquisition or a clever slogan. It came from modest, stubborn leaders who put the right people in place before setting direction, faced the ugliest facts about their position without flinching, and then pushed relentlessly on the one narrow thing they could be best in the world at. No single push looked decisive from the outside. The accumulated weight of them was.

sparks.hook: The best chief executives were ones you would struggle to name.
sparks.insight: The leaders who presided over the largest sustained turnarounds were not the magazine-cover kind. They were awkward, self-effacing people who talked about the company rather than themselves, and who saved their ferocity for the work instead of the spotlight. The mix is the whole point: personal modesty sitting on top of an almost fanatical drive. Ambition was there, but it pointed at the institution rather than the individual. When results were good they credited luck and colleagues. When results were bad they looked in the mirror.
sparks.why: This is a correlation drawn from a small hand-picked sample, so treat it as a hypothesis rather than a law. It is still a useful corrective to the belief that rescue arrives in the form of a celebrity hire.
sparks.apply: In your next team review, name one failure and take the blame yourself before anyone else speaks. Then name one success and credit a specific person for it.

sparks.hook: Decide who is on the bus before you decide where it is going.
sparks.insight: Most plans start with a destination and then recruit people to reach it. The companies that made the leap did the reverse. They gathered an unusually capable, self-motivated group first, moved out the people who did not belong, and only then argued about direction. The logic holds up: a strong team can change course when the world changes, while a weak team executing a brilliant plan simply arrives late somewhere that no longer matters. Strategy is perishable. The people are the durable asset.
sparks.why: It reframes hiring from a support function into the strategy itself. The catch is that it only works if you act quickly on people who do not fit, which is the part almost every manager postpones.
sparks.apply: List everyone reporting to you and mark who you would enthusiastically hire again today. For anyone you would not, book the honest conversation inside two weeks.

carousel.title: Hire ahead of the plan
carousel.body: Recruit for judgement and drive rather than for a role on an org chart you have not finalised. If the person is genuinely excellent, the seat can be invented around them later.

carousel.title: Be rigorous, not ruthless
carousel.body: Rigorous means applying the same high standard to everyone, consistently, including yourself. Ruthless means cutting heads whenever the numbers wobble. The first builds trust, the second destroys it.

carousel.title: Put the best on the biggest chance
carousel.body: Most firms staff their strongest people onto their worst problems. Move at least one of them onto your largest opportunity instead, and accept that the problem may need to be sold or closed.

carousel.title: Stop waiting for improvement
carousel.body: If you are managing someone hard just to get ordinary output, you already know the answer. Delaying the conversation costs the rest of the team more than having it costs you.

sparks.hook: The optimists broke first. The survivors held two beliefs at once.
sparks.insight: The pairing is uncomfortable but necessary: unshakeable faith that you prevail in the end, held at the same time as a refusal to lie to yourself about how bad things are right now. Pure optimism collapses when each hoped-for deadline passes without rescue. Pure realism drains the will to keep working at all. Holding both is unpleasant, which is exactly why it is rare. The example that made the idea famous comes from a US officer held for years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam, who watched hope without honesty destroy the men around him.
sparks.why: This is one vivid anecdote, not evidence, and it has been retold so often that it now functions as folklore. The underlying tension between keeping morale up and keeping the books honest is real in any turnaround.
sparks.apply: Write two columns for your current project: the outcome you genuinely believe in, and the three facts you have been avoiding saying aloud. Then share the second column.

sparks.hook: Three questions, one small answer, and everything outside it gets cut.
sparks.insight: Focus is not picking what you are good at. It is locating the narrow overlap between three separate things: what you could genuinely become the best in the world at, what actually drives your economic engine, and what you and your people care about deeply. Any two without the third builds a business that works for a while and then stops. The overlap is usually far smaller and far less glamorous than the ambitions people bring to the exercise, and it tends to take years to see clearly rather than a weekend offsite.
sparks.why: The discipline lives in the subtraction. Naming the overlap is easy. Killing the profitable but off-strategy lines sitting outside it is the part that separates the companies that changed from the ones that talked about changing.
sparks.apply: Draw the three circles for your business or your career this week, then name one activity that falls outside the overlap and put a date on stopping it.

carousel.title: Test best in the world
carousel.body: Not what you are currently competent at, and not what you wish you were. Ask where you could plausibly become better than anyone else, and accept that the honest answer may be nowhere yet.

carousel.title: Find the economic engine
carousel.body: Identify the single ratio that moves profitability more than any other: profit per customer, per employee, per store, per visit. Knowing which one it is changes where every pound goes.

carousel.title: Check for real passion
carousel.body: Not manufactured enthusiasm from an away day. Ask what work your strongest people would still care about after a bad quarter, because that is what sustains years of unglamorous grinding.

carousel.title: Use it as a filter
carousel.body: The idea only pays off when it starts refusing things. Write a stop-doing list alongside your to-do list and treat the stop list as the more important of the two documents.

sparks.hook: There was never a single moment when the turnaround began.
sparks.insight: Insiders at the transformed companies were often baffled when asked to name the turning point. There was no launch event, no rousing speech, no decisive acquisition. What happened instead was a heavy wheel being pushed in a consistent direction, quarter after quarter, until momentum started doing the work that effort used to do. The outside world only noticed once the wheel was already spinning fast, and then wrote a story about a sudden breakthrough that nobody inside the company recognised.
sparks.why: This is a direct attack on how business media narrates change. It also explains why imported turnaround programmes fail: they supply the announcement without the years of consistent pushing in one direction.
sparks.apply: Name the two or three moves in your business that reinforce each other, then commit to repeating them for four straight quarters before judging whether they work.

sparks.hook: Charisma is a liability if it stops people telling you the truth.
sparks.insight: A leader whose opinion is obvious to the room gets a filtered version of reality, and filtered reality kills companies slowly. The fix is structural rather than personal. Lead with questions instead of answers, argue hard without assigning blame afterwards, and build a channel where inconvenient information reaches the top without being softened on the way up. The aim is not a nicer culture. It is an accurate one, because no amount of courage saves a decision that was made on a sanitised picture.
sparks.why: The mechanism is plain information economics. People withhold bad news when the expected cost of delivering it exceeds the expected benefit. Change that calculation and the news starts arriving early enough to act on.
sparks.apply: At your next meeting, state your own view last rather than first, and thank the person who contradicts you most loudly in front of everyone else.

carousel.title: Ask before you assert
carousel.body: Walk in with questions rather than conclusions. The moment the room knows what you think, you stop receiving information and start receiving agreement dressed up as analysis.

carousel.title: Argue, do not decree
carousel.body: Run real debate with the people who hold the facts, and let it get heated. A decision that has survived genuine argument is much harder to quietly sabotage afterwards.

carousel.title: Autopsy without blame
carousel.body: When something fails, dissect it in public and forbid naming a culprit. Blame teaches people to hide the next failure until it has become expensive to fix.

carousel.title: Build a truth channel
carousel.body: Create one route by which frontline reality reaches you unedited: skip-level sessions, raw complaint logs, a standing agenda item nobody is allowed to summarise for you.

sparks.hook: Technology never made a company great. It magnified what was already there.
sparks.insight: The transformed companies were often early and aggressive adopters, but never for the sake of being modern. They asked one question first: does this fit the narrow thing we have decided to be best at? If yes, they invested hard and early. If no, they ignored it however loudly the market insisted otherwise. Technology behaves like an amplifier bolted onto an existing engine. Attach it to a good engine and you travel faster. Attach it to a bad one and you reach the wall sooner.
sparks.why: Written before smartphones and cloud computing, the claim is less safe than it was. For some incumbents a platform shift genuinely rewrote the economics rather than amplifying them. The filter question survives even so.
sparks.apply: Before approving the next tool or platform, write one sentence explaining how it strengthens the specific advantage you already have. If you cannot write it, decline.

sparks.hook: Bureaucracy exists to compensate for having hired the wrong people.
sparks.insight: Rules multiply in proportion to how much managing your people need. The alternative is to hire people who arrive with their own discipline and then give them a great deal of freedom inside a very tight frame. What makes it work is that the frame really is narrow: everyone knows exactly what the company is and is not doing, so autonomy never turns into drift. Most organisations get the ratio backwards, offering a vague strategy with tight process control, then wondering why their strongest people leave.
sparks.why: The trade-off is real and rarely admitted. This only works at hiring standards most firms will not hold, and it fails badly in settings where process exists for safety rather than for control.
sparks.apply: Find one approval step your team resents. Remove it for a quarter and replace it with a written principle people can apply for themselves.

sparks.hook: Companies on the great list later went bankrupt or needed a bailout.
sparks.insight: The list has not aged kindly. An electronics retailer on it liquidated within a decade. A mortgage giant on it had to be taken into government conservatorship during the financial crisis. A bank on it later became a byword for sales-target scandals. The deeper problem is not luck but method: the companies were selected because they had already outperformed, then examined for shared traits. Do that and you will always find traits, including ones that also show up in the firms that collapsed.
sparks.why: Choosing cases on the outcome and then reasoning backwards cannot establish cause. Critics have also shown that judgements about a company's culture tend to follow its share price rather than predict it.
sparks.apply: Whenever you read a business success study, ask what the failed companies did. If nobody looked, downgrade the conclusion from a finding to a hypothesis worth testing.

sparks.hook: The main obstacle to a great business is a perfectly acceptable one.
sparks.insight: Nothing forces change on an organisation that is doing fine. Adequate results fund adequate habits, and the absence of crisis removes the only pressure most companies reliably respond to. That is why the majority of decent businesses stay decent forever. Escaping means manufacturing the discomfort that reality is not supplying: setting a standard your current setup cannot meet, and being willing to stop activities that are profitable but merely fine. The real choice is rarely between good and bad. It is between good and something harder.
sparks.why: Comfortable performance is a genuine trap because it removes urgency while consuming the resources a change would need. The honest counterpoint is that plenty of businesses should simply stay good and stop reaching.
sparks.apply: Write a stop-doing list of three activities that make money but sit off strategy, and take the smallest one to your board this month.

actions: Run a two-hour session that answers the three focus questions honestly, and close it by naming one profitable activity you will stop doing this year.
Grade every direct report against the test of whether you would hire them again today, and schedule the difficult conversations before you touch the strategy deck.
Write the two or three reinforcing moves that make up your flywheel on a single page, and commit publicly to running them unchanged for four quarters.
Read a serious critique of the study's method next to the book, then re-read your own strategy documents hunting for the same backwards reasoning from outcomes to causes.
not_for_you_if: You want statistically defensible causal claims, or you run a small business and get little from a sample of large American corporations.

verification.notes: Published 2001 by HarperBusiness. Several featured companies later failed or were rescued, and the research design has been widely criticised for selecting cases on the outcome. All prose here is original.

title: Built to Last
subtitle: Successful Habits of Visionary Companies
author: Jim Collins and Jerry I. Porras
why_it_matters: It moved the central question from which product wins to which institution endures, and handed a generation of founders the vocabulary of core purpose and audacious long-range goals. Nearly every mission statement written since owes it something, for better and for worse.

crux.headline: Build the clock, do not just tell the time
crux.body: The companies that lasted a century were rarely built by a visionary individual with a brilliant idea. They were built by people whose real product was the organisation itself: how it selects people, how it promotes them, what it celebrates, how it kills bad ideas. A great idea has a lifespan. A machine that keeps generating and testing ideas does not. Spend your effort on the mechanism, and treat any single strategy as disposable.

sparks.hook: Stop having brilliant ideas. Build the thing that has them for you.
sparks.insight: Founders are usually remembered for one insight, which flatters both them and the story. The longest-lived companies were led by people who behaved more like engineers of an institution than like inventors of a product. Their attention went into structures that would still be producing good decisions after they were dead: how newcomers are chosen, what gets rewarded, which failures are tolerated, how the next leader is grown. A great product buys you a decade. A great mechanism for producing products buys you a century.
sparks.why: It shifts the founder's job from being right to designing a system that keeps being right without them, which is the only version that survives their departure or their next bad call.
sparks.apply: Name one decision you personally make every week. Write down the rule you actually use, hand it to someone else, and stop making that decision.

sparks.hook: Purpose or profit is a false choice, and picking one makes you worse at both.
sparks.insight: Most strategy conversations get framed as a trade-off: values or returns, stability or change, low cost or high quality. The enduring companies treated that framing as a failure of imagination and went looking for arrangements that delivered both ends at once. Sometimes that meant a structural fix, sometimes a slower timeline, sometimes accepting a harder problem. The habit matters more than any individual solution, because a company that reflexively accepts trade-offs stops searching the moment somebody draws a two-column list on a whiteboard.
sparks.why: Trade-offs are often real at a fixed level of ingenuity, and plenty of them genuinely bind. The value here is procedural: refusing the first trade-off you are offered surfaces options nobody had bothered to look for.
sparks.apply: Take the trade-off your team argues about most, and spend thirty minutes generating options that get both sides before you allow anyone to pick one.

sparks.hook: A goal you feel confident about is too small to change the company.
sparks.insight: The enduring companies periodically committed to a goal so large it was slightly embarrassing to state out loud, with a long deadline and no obvious route to it. The point is not the goal itself but what it does to the organisation while it remains unresolved: it makes existing capability visibly insufficient, it forces choices between projects, and it gives ordinary people a reason to argue for something bigger than their own department. A target you already know how to hit organises nothing, because nothing has to change to reach it.
sparks.why: Ambitious public commitments concentrate effort and legitimise saying no to good ideas. The obvious risk is a bet that fails and takes the firm with it, which is why these worked best alongside a conservative balance sheet.
sparks.apply: Write a goal for the next ten years that would take a genuinely different company to achieve, then name the first capability you would have to build.

sparks.hook: The strongest cultures felt slightly uncomfortable to outsiders.
sparks.insight: Enduring companies were not easy-going places to work. They were specific about what they believed, heavy-handed about teaching it to newcomers, and unembarrassed about parting company with people who did not fit. That looks unattractive from outside and it is easily abused, but the effect is real: when everyone shares a genuinely narrow set of beliefs, you can push decisions down without losing coherence. The alternative is a culture broad enough to include everybody, which then has to be enforced by supervision instead.
sparks.why: Tight belief systems substitute for supervision, which is why they scale. The cost is lower tolerance for dissent, and the same mechanism that produces coherence has produced some of the ugliest corporate scandals on record.
sparks.apply: Write the three beliefs someone would have to share to thrive on your team, then test them by naming a good performer who would fail one of them.

carousel.title: State the beliefs narrowly
carousel.body: Values nobody could object to do no work at all. Write beliefs specific enough that a reasonable person at another firm would genuinely disagree with at least one of them.

carousel.title: Teach them on day one
carousel.body: Front-load the induction. New joiners copy whatever they see in their first fortnight, so decide deliberately what that fortnight contains instead of leaving it to whoever is free.

carousel.title: Reward and promote on them
carousel.body: People read promotions, not posters. If someone who ignores the stated beliefs gets promoted for hitting numbers, you have just published your real values to everyone.

carousel.title: Accept the exits
carousel.body: A tight culture will lose capable people who do not fit it, and that is the mechanism working rather than failing. Make the parting quick, generous and honest.

sparks.hook: Some of the best strategies were accidents that nobody bothered to kill.
sparks.insight: Not every successful line of business was planned. Several arrived because somebody was allowed to try something odd, the result was watched rather than judged, and the promising version got funded while the rest were dropped. That is closer to breeding than to architecture. It requires two things most companies only claim to have: genuine permission to run small unauthorised experiments, and the ruthlessness to stop the ones that do not work rather than protecting them because a senior person is attached.
sparks.why: Variation plus selection is a reliable way to find things you could not have predicted. It only produces value when the selection half is real, and killing projects is the half that organisations are worst at.
sparks.apply: Give one person a small budget and a month to try something unapproved, and agree in advance the number that decides whether it continues.

sparks.hook: Almost everything about your company should change. A very small core should not.
sparks.insight: Longevity comes from separating two things most firms blur together. There is a small core of beliefs and purpose that stays fixed for decades and is never traded away for a quarter. Everything else, including products, structures, incentives and strategies, is up for constant revision. Confusing the two is fatal in both directions: companies that treat their operating habits as sacred slowly ossify, and companies with no fixed core drift into whatever looked profitable last year and lose the ability to make hard calls at all.
sparks.why: The distinction gives you a decision rule under pressure. If a change threatens the core, refuse it. If it merely threatens a habit, make the change and stop calling the habit a value.
sparks.apply: Write two lists: what you would keep even if it cost you money for five years, and what you have merely got used to. Then cut one item from the second list.

carousel.title: Find the actual core
carousel.body: Ask what you would still hold if it became a competitive disadvantage. Anything you would abandon under pressure is a preference, not a core belief, and belongs on the other list.

carousel.title: Name the purpose
carousel.body: Write why the organisation exists beyond making money, in language you could say to a sceptical employee without wincing. It should be unreachable, so that it never expires.

carousel.title: Label the rest disposable
carousel.body: Strategies, structures, product lines, pricing, office norms. Say out loud that these are tools, so that changing them is not experienced as a betrayal of identity.

carousel.title: Review on a schedule
carousel.body: Put an annual date in the calendar to challenge the disposable list deliberately. Without a scheduled challenge, ordinary habits quietly get promoted to values.

sparks.hook: The enduring companies almost never hired an outside saviour.
sparks.insight: Continuity of leadership turned out to be a strong marker of longevity. The long-lived firms grew their own successors over decades, so whoever took over already understood which parts of the company were sacred and which were merely tools. Bringing in a celebrated outsider looks decisive and reads well in the press, but it imports somebody who has to learn the core while under pressure to prove they were worth hiring, which is precisely the moment they are most likely to trade the core away.
sparks.why: Internal succession preserves tacit knowledge that no handover document captures. The obvious failure mode is inbreeding, where a firm that genuinely needs to change keeps promoting people who cannot see the problem.
sparks.apply: Name the two internal candidates who could do your job in three years, and hand each of them one real piece of it this quarter.

sparks.hook: Comfortable is what a company feels like just before it stops mattering.
sparks.insight: The long-lived firms built in mechanisms that made contentment difficult: internal targets that outpaced the market, deliberate cannibalisation of their own products, and comparisons against the best rather than against last year. None of this was a response to crisis. It was installed while things were going well, precisely because that is when nobody wants it and when the resources to act still exist. Discomfort by design is cheaper than discomfort by circumstance, and you get to choose the timing.
sparks.why: Organisations respond to pressure, and if the market is not supplying any you have to manufacture it. The risk is manufactured urgency that exhausts people without changing anything, which is how most transformation programmes fail.
sparks.apply: Pick your most successful product and assign someone the explicit job of designing the thing that would replace it, with a real budget attached.

sparks.hook: Several of the visionary companies later became case studies in decline.
sparks.insight: Within two decades of publication some of the celebrated firms had lost their industries outright. A mobile phone pioneer on the list was broken up after missing the smartphone. A consumer electronics giant on it spent years being beaten by newer rivals. A carmaker on the list needed emergency financing. That does not make the observations worthless, but it does undercut the promise in the title, and it shows how much of what looked like a durable trait was really a description of a good run.
sparks.why: The study picked companies that had already succeeded and then searched for shared characteristics, so the traits could never be tested against firms that had the same traits and failed anyway.
sparks.apply: Before adopting a practice because a great company uses it, find two failing companies that also use it. If you find them, treat the practice as neutral.

sparks.hook: A purpose that helps you win customers is probably not a purpose.
sparks.insight: Core purpose gets confused with positioning, and the two behave completely differently. Positioning points outward and exists to differentiate you from competitors, so it changes as they change. Purpose points inward, is allowed to be unoriginal, and exists to tell people inside the building what matters when a decision is genuinely hard. Two rival firms can honestly share the same purpose. If yours reads like it came out of a marketing brief, it will not survive the first quarter in which honouring it costs real money.
sparks.why: The test is behavioural rather than verbal. A stated purpose only counts if you can point to a decision where you gave up revenue to keep it. Otherwise it is decoration on a wall.
sparks.apply: Find the last decision where your stated purpose cost you money. If there is not one, either rewrite the purpose or stop displaying it.

actions: Separate your values into two written lists: the small core you would defend at real cost, and the operating habits you have simply grown used to.
Design one mechanism that will keep making a good decision after you leave, then hand a decision you currently own over to that mechanism this month.
Commit to a ten-year goal your current organisation could not achieve, and name the first capability gap that the commitment exposes.
Audit your succession bench by naming two internal candidates for your role and giving each of them a real piece of it this quarter.
not_for_you_if: You want tested causal evidence, or you run a young company where a hundred-year view of large corporations is not yet the pressing problem.

verification.notes: First published 1994 by HarperBusiness. Several of the profiled companies later declined sharply, and the study design has been criticised for selecting on the outcome. All prose here is original.

title: Competitive Strategy
subtitle: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors
author: Michael E. Porter
why_it_matters: It gave strategy an analytical spine. Before it, competitive advantage was mostly anecdote and instinct; after it, managers had a repeatable way to work out where profit in an industry actually sits and why some sectors are structurally miserable no matter how well you run your firm.

crux.headline: Profit lives in industry structure, not in effort
crux.body: How much money you can make is set mostly by the shape of the industry you are in and the position you hold inside it. Five pressures decide it: rivals fighting you, new entrants arriving, substitutes making you unnecessary, buyers squeezing your price, suppliers taking your margin. Working harder inside a bad structure produces a well-run business with terrible returns. Strategy is choosing where to stand so those pressures fall on somebody else.

sparks.hook: Some industries make almost nobody rich, however well they are run.
sparks.insight: Average profitability varies enormously between industries and stays that way for decades, which tells you something is structural rather than managerial. Five pressures determine how much of the value created in an industry the firms in it actually keep. Understanding them stops you blaming execution for a problem that is really about position. It also tells you where to aim: a change that weakens one of the five pressures is worth far more than a change that makes you marginally more efficient at fighting inside the existing structure.
sparks.why: The framework's staying power comes from being descriptive rather than prescriptive. It does not tell you what to do, it tells you where the money is going, which is usually the question people skip.
sparks.apply: Score each of the five pressures on your own industry from one to five this week, then plan your next move against the two scoring highest.

carousel.title: Map rivalry
carousel.body: How many comparable competitors, how similar the offers, how fast the market grows, how costly it is to exit. Slow growth plus high exit barriers produces the worst price wars.

carousel.title: Test entry
carousel.body: Ask what a well-funded newcomer would need: capital, licences, a brand, a distribution deal, scale. If the honest answer is not much, your current margins are borrowed.

carousel.title: Hunt substitutes
carousel.body: Not rival products but different answers to the same need. A video call substitutes for a flight. Substitutes cap your price long before a direct competitor does.

carousel.title: Weigh buyer power
carousel.body: Concentrated buyers with low switching costs and good information will take your margin. Count what share of revenue your largest few customers represent.

carousel.title: Weigh supplier power
carousel.body: A supplier with few alternatives, a strong brand or the ability to move into your business sets your input costs. Check where you have no second source.

sparks.hook: Your competitors are not the only ones taking your profit.
sparks.insight: Managers watch rivals obsessively and barely notice the other four routes by which money leaves the industry. A single dominant customer can dictate terms until you are working for a wage. A supplier with no substitute can raise prices every year and you will pay. A newcomer can arrive because nothing stopped them. And a technology that answers the same need differently can cap what anyone is allowed to charge. All four are competition. They just do not appear on the list of firms you benchmark against.
sparks.why: It widens the definition of competition from firms that resemble you to anyone who can capture value you created. That reframing catches threats that competitor benchmarking structurally cannot see.
sparks.apply: List the five largest claims on your gross margin, only one of which may be a direct competitor, and name the weakest one you could fix this year.

sparks.hook: Be the cheapest or be genuinely different. Halfway is the losing spot.
sparks.insight: There are only a few coherent ways to hold a position. You can be the lowest-cost producer and use that to survive price competition everyone else loses money on. You can be different in a way buyers will pay a premium for. Or you can do either of those inside one narrow segment rather than the whole market. What does not work is a bit of both, because the moves that lower cost usually undercut differentiation and vice versa. Firms without a clear answer end up with structurally worse margins than either pure option.
sparks.why: The trap is real, though the strict either-or has been challenged: several firms have combined low cost with strong differentiation by rethinking the operating model rather than splitting the difference between two existing ones.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence stating whether you win on cost or on difference, then find the last three decisions that contradicted it.

carousel.title: Cost leadership
carousel.body: Be structurally cheaper to run than anyone else through scale, process or asset choices. Note that being cheapest is not the same as charging least; the advantage is surviving a price war.

carousel.title: Differentiation
carousel.body: Be valued for something buyers will pay extra for and rivals cannot easily copy: reliability, design, service, brand, an ecosystem. It must be defensible, not merely nice.

carousel.title: Focus on a segment
carousel.body: Apply either approach to a slice of the market you can serve better than a generalist. A narrow position is often the only viable one for a smaller firm.

carousel.title: Avoid the middle
carousel.body: Check whether your last five investments pulled in opposite directions. A cost cut that damages your premium and a feature that raises your cost base leaves you beaten from both sides.

sparks.hook: A profitable business without barriers is just a well-publicised invitation.
sparks.insight: If you have found something lucrative and easy to copy, you have effectively advertised it. What protects returns is whatever makes imitation expensive or slow: scale you already have and a newcomer does not, a brand customers trust, switching costs, exclusive distribution, patents, or a cost position built up over years of learning. Barriers are also not permanent. They erode, and some of the strongest ones in the twentieth century have been dissolved by cheap distribution over the internet.
sparks.why: Entry barriers are the difference between a temporarily good business and a durably good one. The honest caveat is that many modern barriers, particularly network effects and data scale, sit awkwardly inside a framework written before them.
sparks.apply: Write down what a funded competitor would have to spend and how long they would need to match you. If the answer is under a year, build a barrier before you expand.

sparks.hook: One customer worth a third of your revenue is not a customer. It is a boss.
sparks.insight: Buyer power decides how much of the value you create you actually keep. It rises when buyers are few and large, when what you sell is undifferentiated, when they can easily switch, when they know your costs, and when they could credibly make it themselves. Each of those is a lever you can push on. You can deliberately diversify your customer base, build switching costs, differentiate the offer, or make your pricing harder to decompose. Concentration feels like success right up until renewal.
sparks.why: Customer concentration is one of the few strategic risks with a clean number attached to it, which is why acquirers and lenders check it before anything else in the accounts.
sparks.apply: Calculate the revenue share of your top three customers today. If any single one is above twenty percent, put a named diversification target in the plan.

sparks.hook: Inside one industry there are several games, and you are only in one.
sparks.insight: Firms in the same industry cluster into groups that play similar strategies: the premium specialists, the volume discounters, the regional operators. Competition inside a group is fierce, competition between groups is muted, and moving from one group to another is far harder than it looks because it requires assets and habits you do not have. That is why a discounter attempting to go upmarket usually fails. Knowing which group you are actually in tells you who your real rivals are and what a move would genuinely cost.
sparks.why: It explains why firms in one industry can show persistently different profitability. The obstacles between groups are made of sunk investment and reputation, which is why they resist strategy decks.
sparks.apply: Plot the firms in your industry on two axes such as price and breadth, then circle your group and name the two rivals actually in it.

sparks.hook: Predicting a rival's move is a research problem, not a guessing game.
sparks.insight: Most competitor analysis stops at a feature comparison, which tells you what a rival sells but nothing about what they will do next. What predicts behaviour is four things: what they are actually trying to achieve, what they believe about the industry and about themselves, what they are doing now, and what they are physically capable of. A rival with an unrealistic belief about their own position is predictable and exploitable. A rival with a different goal from yours may not respond to your price cut at all.
sparks.why: Behaviour follows goals and beliefs rather than capability alone, which is why firms with similar resources respond to the same provocation in opposite ways. Where you can, verify beliefs from public statements rather than assuming them.
sparks.apply: Pick your most dangerous rival and write half a page on each of their goals, beliefs, current strategy and capabilities before your next planning meeting.

carousel.title: Establish their goals
carousel.body: Are they optimising for growth, margin, share or survival? A private firm chasing cash and a listed firm defending share will react to the same price move very differently.

carousel.title: Surface their assumptions
carousel.body: What do they believe about the market and their own standing? Public statements, hiring patterns and investor calls expose beliefs that are often several years out of date.

carousel.title: Describe their current strategy
carousel.body: Not what they say, but what their spending shows. Where the money and headcount go tells you which claims are real and which are aspiration.

carousel.title: Assess their capabilities
carousel.body: What could they actually execute within a year given their cost base, technology and distribution? A threat they cannot resource is not a threat this planning cycle.

sparks.hook: A price announcement is a message, and rivals read it more carefully than customers.
sparks.insight: Public moves in a concentrated industry carry information beyond their immediate commercial effect. Pre-announcing a product, floating a price rise, publicly committing to defend a segment: all of these tell competitors what you intend and invite them to adjust rather than fight. Reading these signals is how you tell an aggressive move from a bluff. Sending them deliberately is how you avoid a destructive war neither side wanted. This is also legally sensitive territory, and coordinating on price with rivals is illegal in most jurisdictions.
sparks.why: Signalling matters most where a few firms interact repeatedly, because each expects to meet the other again. Read it as a reason to interpret rival announcements as communication rather than as fact.
sparks.apply: Before your next public price or product announcement, write what a competitor will conclude from it and decide whether that is the message you want sent.

sparks.hook: Every good position is temporary, because the structure underneath it moves.
sparks.insight: Industries evolve in ways that shift where profit sits. Growth slows and rivalry turns to price. Buyers become experienced and stop paying for reassurance. Products standardise and differentiation stops working. Distribution channels consolidate and start taking a bigger share. A position that was excellent ten years ago can become the worst place to stand without anyone at the firm making a mistake. So the analysis is not a one-off exercise; it is something to rerun when the underlying conditions change, not when your results do.
sparks.why: Structural change is slow and therefore easy to miss inside annual planning cycles that compare this year with last year. By the time results move, the repositioning window has usually narrowed.
sparks.apply: Redo your five-pressure scoring once a year and compare it with last year's. Act on any pressure that moved by two points or more.

sparks.hook: The framework is a snapshot, and it was drawn before platforms existed.
sparks.insight: The main criticisms are worth holding alongside the tools. The analysis is essentially static, describing an industry at a moment rather than a system in motion. It says little about complements, the products that make yours more valuable, which is where much of the value in software and platforms now sits. It treats industry boundaries as clearer than they are. And a rival school argues that advantage comes from what a firm uniquely owns and knows, not from where it sits. Use it as a lens, not a verdict.
sparks.why: None of these objections show the pressures are absent; they show the picture is incomplete. Pairing structural analysis with a hard look at your own distinctive capabilities catches most of what either misses alone.
sparks.apply: After your structural analysis, list the three capabilities only you have and check whether your chosen position actually uses any of them.

actions: Score all five competitive pressures on your industry, write one page on the two strongest, and take that page to your next planning session.
State in one sentence whether you compete on cost or on difference, then audit your last ten decisions for ones that pulled the other way.
Calculate the revenue share of your three largest customers and your dependence on any single-source supplier, and set a target for the worst of the two.
Build a one-page profile of your most dangerous rival covering their goals, beliefs, current spending and realistic capabilities.
not_for_you_if: You want quick tactics rather than analysis, or you work in a fast-moving platform market where industry boundaries are genuinely unstable.

verification.notes: First published 1980 by Free Press. The framework has been criticised as static and for underweighting complements and network effects. All prose here is original.

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
subtitle: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail
author: Clayton M. Christensen
why_it_matters: It explained why competent, well-run market leaders lose to worse products made by smaller firms, and it did so with a mechanism rather than a moral. The word disruption entered every boardroom because of it, usually misused.

crux.headline: The things that make you strong are what kill you
crux.body: Leading firms fail not by being lazy but by being disciplined. They listen to their best customers, invest where the margins are highest, and refuse small markets that cannot move their numbers. Those are correct decisions. They are also precisely the decisions that make a cheaper, simpler, lower-margin product impossible to pursue until a smaller firm has ridden it up into your market and taken it.

sparks.hook: The market leaders that lost were not badly run. That is the whole problem.
sparks.insight: The comfortable explanation for a fallen giant is arrogance, bureaucracy or laziness. The uncomfortable finding is that the firms which lost their markets were often the most capable ones, and they lost by following the advice that every management textbook gives. They stayed close to their customers, invested in the highest-return projects, and improved their products faster than anyone. The failure was not an error in execution. It was the correct application of good practice to a situation where good practice points the wrong way.
sparks.why: This is what makes the argument uncomfortable and useful. If failure required a mistake, avoiding mistakes would be enough. Because it does not, avoiding failure requires a deliberate structural exception.
sparks.apply: Name one project your normal approval process would reject that a smaller rival is already doing. Ask why your process says no.

sparks.hook: The technology that kills you starts out worse than what you already sell.
sparks.insight: Most innovation improves a product along the dimensions existing customers already value, and incumbents almost always win that race because they have more resources and more reason to run it. The dangerous kind is different. It performs worse on the established measures but better on some other axis, usually cheaper, smaller, simpler or more convenient. Your best customers reject it, correctly, and your own analysis confirms it is inferior. That is exactly why nobody at your firm can build a case for taking it seriously.
sparks.why: The distinction is between competing on the existing scoreboard and changing which scoreboard matters. Firms are structurally good at the first and structurally blind to the second.
sparks.apply: List the cheap, limited products your customers currently laugh at, and pick the one improving fastest to track every quarter.

sparks.hook: Listening to your best customers is how you get led off a cliff politely.
sparks.insight: Your largest customers fund your business, so their wishes shape your roadmap whether or not anyone decides that. They will ask for more of what they already buy, faster and better, because that is what their own operations need. They will not ask for the cheap simple thing that serves people they do not care about. So a customer-led company is systematically steered away from the only market where the next threat is growing. The pull is financial, not psychological, which is why willpower does not fix it.
sparks.why: Resource allocation follows revenue. In practice the decision is made by dozens of middle managers choosing safe projects that clear the hurdle rate, long before it reaches anyone senior enough to overrule it.
sparks.apply: Ask your five largest customers what they would never buy from you. Treat the most common answer as a market description rather than a rejection.

sparks.hook: Products improve faster than people's needs, and then good enough wins.
sparks.insight: Competition pushes established firms to keep adding performance year after year. Customer requirements rise far more slowly. Eventually the mainstream product overshoots what most buyers actually use, and the extra capability stops being worth paying for. At that moment the basis of competition quietly changes from performance to price, convenience or simplicity, and the cheap alternative that was never good enough becomes good enough. The incumbent, still winning on the old measure, does not notice that the measure stopped mattering.
sparks.why: Overshoot is the engine of the whole argument, and it is observable. When customers stop upgrading and start asking for discounts, capability has run past need.
sparks.apply: Find one feature your last three releases improved and check what share of customers actually use it. If it is small, you are overshooting.

sparks.hook: Disruption almost always arrives from below, never from beside you.
sparks.insight: The threat does not appear as a better version of your product at a similar price. It appears at the bottom, serving customers you were happy to lose or people who previously bought nothing at all because everything available was too expensive or too complicated. It makes poor money there, which is exactly why you ignore it. Then it improves, as everything does, and climbs into the segments you do care about carrying a cost structure you cannot match. By the time it is a competitor, it is too late to become one.
sparks.why: The pattern repeats because upward improvement is easy and downward repositioning is hard. Moving up market means better margins for the newcomer and a shrinking retreat for you.
sparks.apply: Identify who cannot afford or cannot use your product today. Check every six months whether anyone is now serving them adequately.

sparks.hook: A market big enough to matter to you is already too big to enter first.
sparks.insight: A large company needs growth in proportion to its size, so an opportunity has to be substantial before it is worth the attention of senior people. But emerging markets are by definition small, and they stay small for years before they are not. This produces a trap with no internal solution: by the time a new market is large enough to justify your involvement, it has been claimed by firms that entered when it was still trivial. The arithmetic, not the culture, is what excludes you.
sparks.why: This is a straightforward consequence of size and is why acquisitions so often replace organic entry. The counterpoint is that many small markets stay small, so entering them all is not a strategy either.
sparks.apply: Calculate the smallest revenue a new project needs to get funded at your firm. Anything below that line is territory you have conceded.

sparks.hook: You cannot research a market that does not exist yet, so stop trying.
sparks.insight: Established firms plan by forecasting, which works when there is history to forecast from. For a genuinely new market there is no history, the early estimates are almost always wrong in both directions, and the first product usually finds its real use somewhere the team never considered. The right posture is to spend as little as possible learning what the market actually is, and to keep enough resource in reserve to fund the second attempt, since the second attempt is usually the one that works.
sparks.why: The prescription is to plan for learning rather than for execution. Its weakness is that it can excuse indefinite experimentation, so each round needs a written question and a decision point.
sparks.apply: For your next new-market bet, write the single assumption you are least sure of and the cheapest test that could disprove it within a month.

carousel.title: Write the assumption
carousel.body: State plainly who you think will buy this and why. A forecast is a stack of assumptions with a number on top; name the one holding the most weight.

carousel.title: Buy information cheaply
carousel.body: Design the smallest real-world test that would move your belief. The purpose of the first launch is to find out what the product is for, not to hit a revenue target.

carousel.title: Expect to be wrong
carousel.body: Budget for the second and third attempt from the start. Firms that spend everything on a confident first launch have no capacity left when the real market appears.

carousel.title: Follow the surprise
carousel.body: Watch who buys it for reasons you did not plan. Unexpected usage is the strongest signal you will get about where the market actually is.

sparks.hook: You cannot fix this inside the company. You have to build a smaller one.
sparks.insight: The obstacle is not attitude, it is the cost structure and the size of numbers a large organisation needs to care. A project that would be exciting in a small independent unit is a rounding error in a large one, and it will lose every internal fight for people and budget. The workable answer is to create a separate organisation small enough to be excited by small wins, with its own cost base, its own targets, and enough distance that the parent's processes cannot quietly strangle it.
sparks.why: This is the most contested part of the argument, because separated units often lose access to the capabilities that made the parent strong. Deciding what to share and what to isolate is the real work.
sparks.apply: If you back a low-end product, give it its own budget line, its own profit target and a leader who does not report through the main business.

carousel.title: Size the unit to the market
carousel.body: Make the team small enough that a modest early win is genuinely meaningful to them. Excitement about small numbers cannot be manufactured in a large division.

carousel.title: Give it its own economics
carousel.body: Let it run at margins your main business would reject. Applying the parent's hurdle rate guarantees the project dies at its first review.

carousel.title: Separate the reporting
carousel.body: Keep it out of the main hierarchy, where it competes for resources against established products with better forecasts and louder sponsors.

carousel.title: Decide what to share
carousel.body: Borrow the parent's genuine advantages such as manufacturing or distribution, but not its processes, planning cycle or approval thresholds.

sparks.hook: Your margins are not a fact about you. They are a fact about who you serve.
sparks.insight: Every firm sits in a web of customers, suppliers and channels that together set what costs are normal and what margins are acceptable. Serve demanding high-end customers and you build an expensive operation to match, which then makes cheap work genuinely unprofitable for you rather than merely unattractive. That is why incumbents cannot simply choose to compete at the low end. The cost base is a consequence of the customers, and changing customers means changing almost everything else first.
sparks.why: It explains why the obvious advice to just launch a budget version usually fails. The budget product inherits an overhead structure designed for a different business and loses money honestly.
sparks.apply: Work out your fully loaded cost to serve one customer, then check whether a low-end version could ever be profitable inside that number.

sparks.hook: The theory is now used to describe almost anything, which has weakened it.
sparks.insight: Two honest caveats belong with the argument. First, the original evidence came largely from one industry with unusually fast performance improvement, and later attempts to test the pattern more broadly have produced mixed results, including a well-known critique arguing that several of the historical cases do not fit. Second, the word has been stretched until it means any new company doing well, which drains it of predictive content. It remains a good explanation of one specific failure mode, not a general theory of competition.
sparks.why: The mechanism can be sound while the label is abused. Ask whether a challenger genuinely started worse on the established measures and cheaper. If it started better and pricier, this is not the pattern you are looking at.
sparks.apply: Before calling anything disruptive, check that it began worse on your customers' main measure. If it began better, treat it as ordinary competition and respond directly.

actions: Write down the minimum revenue a new project needs to get funded at your firm, and treat everything below that threshold as territory you have already conceded.
Track the cheapest, most limited product in your market every quarter, recording how fast it is improving rather than how good it is today.
Check what share of customers use the features your last three releases added, to see whether you are overshooting what people need.
If you pursue a low-end opportunity, house it in a separate unit with its own economics and a leader outside the main reporting line.
not_for_you_if: You want a general theory of why companies fail, or you need practical guidance for a small firm rather than an explanation of incumbent behaviour.

verification.notes: First published 1997 by Harvard Business School Press. The core evidence came largely from the disk drive industry, and the theory's historical cases and predictive record have both been publicly disputed. All prose here is original.

title: Blue Ocean Strategy
subtitle: How to Create Uncontested Market Space and Make the Competition Irrelevant
author: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne
why_it_matters: It argued that the most valuable strategic move is not beating rivals but changing what the industry competes on at all, and it supplied tools simple enough that a team could run them in an afternoon. That combination is why it spread so far beyond business schools.

crux.headline: Stop fighting for the market. Redraw it
crux.body: Competing head-on with similar firms grinds margins down until the whole industry is poor. The alternative is to change the set of factors an industry competes on: drop the expensive things buyers do not actually value, and add things nobody currently offers. Done properly this lowers your cost and raises buyer value at the same time, which is why it escapes the usual choice between being cheap and being premium.

sparks.hook: Every rival you beat leaves you in a market worth slightly less.
sparks.insight: When firms compete by matching each other, the offers converge, buyers start choosing on price, and the profit pool shrinks for everyone still in the fight. Winning that contest gets you a larger share of something increasingly worthless. The alternative is to stop treating the industry's existing terms as fixed. Ask which factors everyone competes on because of habit rather than because buyers care, and you usually find several expensive ones that could be dropped without anybody complaining.
sparks.why: Convergence towards a shared definition of quality is well documented in mature industries. The mechanism is imitation: each firm benchmarks the others, so the benchmark becomes the ceiling for everyone.
sparks.apply: List the factors every firm in your industry competes on. Circle any that customers have never once mentioned to you unprompted.

sparks.hook: Cheaper or better is a false pair. The good moves do both.
sparks.insight: Conventional strategy says you pick low cost or high differentiation, because getting more of one costs you the other. That holds only if you keep the industry's existing set of features and adjust the dials. Once you are willing to remove factors entirely, the arithmetic changes: cutting a costly thing buyers do not value releases money to fund something new that they do. The result is an offer that is genuinely cheaper to produce and genuinely more valuable to the buyer, which no rival can match by adjusting price.
sparks.why: The saving has to be real and structural, not a discount. Where the removed factors turn out to matter more than expected, this becomes an ordinary cost cut with a story attached to it.
sparks.apply: Name the single most expensive feature of your offer, then estimate what share of customers would notice if it disappeared tomorrow.

sparks.hook: Four questions turn a feature list into a different business.
sparks.insight: The practical core is a set of moves applied to the factors your industry competes on. Some should be removed outright because they exist only through convention. Some should be reduced well below the standard because everyone has been overdelivering. Some should be raised well above the standard because buyers care more than the industry admits. And some factors nobody currently offers should be created. Doing only the first two gives you a discounter. Doing only the last two gives you an expensive premium product. The combination is the point.
sparks.why: It works because it forces subtraction, which strategy exercises almost never do. Most planning sessions generate additions, and additions raise cost without changing what the business is.
sparks.apply: Run the four moves on your own offer this week and require at least one factor in the remove column before anyone proposes something to add.

carousel.title: Remove
carousel.body: Which factors does your industry compete on that could be dropped altogether? Usually these survive because rivals have them, not because buyers ever asked for them.

carousel.title: Reduce
carousel.body: Which factors are overdelivered relative to what buyers actually use? Cutting these back below the industry standard frees money without any felt loss of value.

carousel.title: Raise
carousel.body: Which factors should go well above the industry standard because buyers quietly tolerate a compromise everyone has stopped noticing?

carousel.title: Create
carousel.body: What could you offer that nobody in the industry does? This is where new demand comes from, and it is the hardest of the four to answer honestly.

sparks.hook: Draw your strategy on one chart and the copying becomes obvious.
sparks.insight: Plot the factors your industry competes on along the bottom of a chart, and how much each firm offers of each one up the side. Join the dots and you get a shape for every competitor. In most industries those shapes sit almost on top of each other, which is a picture of an industry that has stopped making choices. A genuinely different strategy looks different on the chart: low where others are high, high where others are absent. If your line tracks everyone else's, you do not have a strategy, you have a position in a queue.
sparks.why: The value of the chart is that it is hard to argue with. A team can debate strategy abstractly for months, but a picture showing your line sitting on your rival's line ends the discussion quickly.
sparks.apply: Draw the chart for your industry with five to eight factors, plot yourself and two rivals, and show it to your leadership team unedited.

sparks.hook: The biggest market is the people who have never bought from anyone.
sparks.insight: Most marketing digs deeper into existing customers, segmenting them more finely and serving them more precisely. That grows share but not the market. The larger prize is usually the people who are not buying at all: those who use your category reluctantly and would leave if something better appeared, those who considered it and refused, and those who never thought the category was for them. Their reasons for staying away tell you exactly which factors to remove and which to create.
sparks.why: Non-buyers are systematically underweighted because no research process routinely contacts them. They are also easier to learn from than customers, because their objections are concrete and unhedged.
sparks.apply: Interview five people who considered your category and did not buy, and write down the specific reason each gave rather than a summary.

carousel.title: Find the reluctant users
carousel.body: People who buy occasionally and would stop tomorrow if an alternative existed. They already know the category, so their complaints are precise and immediately actionable.

carousel.title: Find the refusers
carousel.body: People who evaluated your category and consciously chose against it. Ask what the deciding factor was, and expect the answer to be price, complexity or time rather than features.

carousel.title: Find the unexplored
carousel.body: People who have never considered the category because nobody markets to them. This group is usually the largest and the hardest to reach, and it is where genuinely new demand sits.

carousel.title: Look for the shared objection
carousel.body: Pool the reasons across all three groups. Where the same barrier appears in all of them, you have found the factor worth removing rather than improving.

sparks.hook: Set the price before you calculate the cost, not after.
sparks.insight: The usual sequence is to build the thing, add a margin and see what the market says. That works for incremental products and fails for new ones, because a new offer needs volume quickly to build reputation and deter imitators. So reverse the order. Decide the price that would attract a large number of buyers straight away, subtract the margin you need, and treat the remainder as a cost target the operation has to be designed to hit. If it cannot hit it, you have learned that early rather than after launch.
sparks.why: Pricing from cost upward tends to produce an offer priced for the enthusiasts, which is precisely the segment that will not generate the scale a new category needs.
sparks.apply: Pick the price that would make your offer obvious to a mass buyer, subtract your required margin, and ask your team whether they could build to that number.

sparks.hook: A new idea has to clear four gates, and most people only check one.
sparks.insight: A genuinely different offer fails for four distinct reasons, and testing them in the wrong order wastes years. First, does it deliver something buyers exceptionally want? Second, is the price reachable for the mass of them? Third, can you produce it profitably at that price? Fourth, will the people who must adopt it — staff, partners, distributors, regulators — actually cooperate? Most teams check the first and the third, then discover too late that the fourth was the binding constraint all along.
sparks.why: Ordering matters because each gate is cheaper to test than the one before it is to build. Adoption resistance in particular is invisible in a business case and decisive in reality.
sparks.apply: Take your current big idea and write one page per gate: buyer value, mass price, cost feasibility, and who will resist. Test the weakest gate first.

carousel.title: Test buyer value
carousel.body: Is there an exceptional reason for someone to want this? If the honest answer is that it is somewhat better, stop here rather than optimising the price of something nobody needs.

carousel.title: Set a mass price
carousel.body: Choose a price that pulls in the bulk of buyers rather than the enthusiasts. New categories need volume to build trust and to make imitation unattractive.

carousel.title: Prove the cost
carousel.body: Work backwards from price to the cost you must hit, then redesign the operation until you reach it. Do not adjust the price to fit the cost you happen to have.

carousel.title: Name the resisters
carousel.body: List every group whose cooperation you need: staff, partners, channels, regulators. Talk to the most sceptical one before you commit, because their objection will not soften later.

sparks.hook: People accept a decision they hate if they understand how it was made.
sparks.insight: Big strategic shifts fail inside organisations more often than in the market, and usually not because the logic was wrong. People resist when a decision arrives without explanation and without any route by which their view could have mattered. Three things fix most of it: involve the people affected while the decision is still open, explain the reasoning including the options you rejected, and state clearly what is now expected of them. None of this requires agreement. It requires that the process was visible.
sparks.why: Perceived fairness of process affects cooperation independently of whether people like the outcome. That is why identical decisions produce compliance in one organisation and quiet sabotage in another.
sparks.apply: Before announcing your next big change, write the options you rejected and why, and include that in the announcement rather than only the conclusion.

sparks.hook: The showcase examples were chosen after they had already won.
sparks.insight: The main criticism is the familiar one. Cases were selected because they succeeded, then examined for a shared pattern, so we never see the firms that redrew their industry's factors and went bankrupt anyway. Several celebrated examples have also had difficult later chapters, including a circus company that sought bankruptcy protection during the pandemic. The tools are still worth running, because forcing a team to subtract is valuable regardless. Treat the case studies as illustrations rather than as proof that the method produces the outcome.
sparks.why: Retrospective case selection cannot show a method causes success, only that successful firms can be described using it. Independent tests of whether the approach raises the odds are thin.
sparks.apply: When you run these tools, note down the assumptions your new position depends on, and set a date to check whether any of them turned out false.

sparks.hook: New space does not stay uncontested. Plan for the copying now.
sparks.insight: A successful redrawing of an industry advertises itself. Imitators arrive, and the more purely the advantage rests on a clever configuration of features rather than on something hard to replicate, the faster they arrive. The durable versions pair the new position with something that resists copying: scale, a brand people trust, a network that gets better with size, or an operating model that a rival cannot adopt without wrecking their existing business. Without one of those, you have bought yourself a few good years.
sparks.why: The framework is strong on finding a new position and weak on defending one. Pairing it with a hard look at barriers to imitation covers the gap it leaves open.
sparks.apply: For your new position, write what a well-funded rival would have to give up to copy you. If the answer is nothing, build a barrier before you scale.

actions: Draw the strategy chart for your industry with the factors everyone competes on, plot yourself against two rivals, and show the result to your leadership team.
Run the four moves on your own offer, and refuse to let anyone propose an addition until at least one factor has been put in the remove column.
Interview five people who considered your category and did not buy, recording their exact reason rather than a summary of it.
Set the price you would need to reach a mass buyer, work backwards to the cost target, and ask whether your operation could be redesigned to hit it.
not_for_you_if: You want evidence that the method causes success rather than describes it, or you need help defending a position you already hold.

verification.notes: First published 2005 by Harvard Business School Press, with an expanded edition in 2015. Case selection is retrospective and several featured firms had difficult later years. All prose here is original.

title: The Lean Startup
subtitle: How Today's Entrepreneurs Use Continuous Innovation to Create Radically Successful Businesses
author: Eric Ries
why_it_matters: It replaced the business plan with the experiment as the basic unit of startup work, and gave a whole industry its shared vocabulary. Corporate innovation teams, accelerators and product organisations still run on the loop it popularised.

crux.headline: Progress is learning, not shipping
crux.body: A new venture is not a small version of a company. It is an organisation searching for a business model under real uncertainty, which means its output is not features but answers. The discipline is to identify the belief your plan most depends on, build the smallest thing that tests it, measure what actually happened rather than what you hoped, and then decide honestly whether to change direction or continue.

sparks.hook: Shipping a lot is not progress if nobody wanted any of it.
sparks.insight: Teams measure themselves by output because output is visible and satisfying: features released, tickets closed, hours worked. Under genuine uncertainty that measure is worthless, because you can execute a plan flawlessly and build something nobody wants. The alternative unit of progress is what you now know that you did not know last month, backed by evidence rather than by opinion. It is a much less comfortable measure, since a productive month can end with the conclusion that the original idea was wrong.
sparks.why: The reframing matters because it changes what gets rewarded. Teams graded on shipping will ship. Teams graded on validated answers will ask better questions and kill weak ideas earlier.
sparks.apply: At the end of this month, write what you learned rather than what you shipped. If the list is empty, you ran no real experiments.

sparks.hook: Your plan rests on two beliefs. Everything else is detail.
sparks.insight: Under the whole business case sit a small number of assumptions that have to be true or nothing works. Two matter most: whether people will actually get value from the thing once they use it, and whether you have a repeatable way for more of them to arrive. Everything else in the plan is derived from those. Naming them explicitly is uncomfortable, because it exposes how much of a confident forecast is resting on a belief nobody has tested and everyone has been assuming.
sparks.why: Isolating the load-bearing assumptions tells you what to test first. Most teams test the safe assumptions because those experiments are pleasant and the results are reassuring.
sparks.apply: Write the two assumptions your plan cannot survive without, then design one cheap test for whichever of them you have the least evidence for.

sparks.hook: Build the smallest thing that could prove you wrong.
sparks.insight: The first version is not a small product. It is an instrument for answering one question, and it should contain nothing that does not serve that question. Sometimes it is a rough product, sometimes a page describing something that does not exist yet, sometimes a service delivered by hand behind the scenes. The bar is not quality or completeness but whether the result would change your mind. If a positive result and a negative result would both lead you to carry on regardless, you have not designed a test.
sparks.why: The concept is widely misused as an excuse for shipping something poor. The real criterion is informational: the smallest build that produces a decision, which is often smaller and sometimes larger than a rough product.
sparks.apply: Before your next build, write the result that would make you abandon the idea. If you cannot write it, redesign the test rather than the product.

sparks.hook: The loop only pays off if you run it faster than your competitors think.
sparks.insight: The cycle is simple to state and hard to run: turn an idea into something you can put in front of people, measure what they do with it, learn from the result, and start again. The advantage comes from the time it takes you to go round once. A team that completes the loop weekly will out-learn a team that completes it quarterly regardless of who is smarter, because they get more chances to be wrong cheaply. So the thing to optimise is not any single stage but the total time from question to answer.
sparks.why: Learning rate compounds in the same way that interest does. Halving your cycle time doubles the number of wrong turns you can afford before running out of money.
sparks.apply: Measure how many days pass between forming a question and having data on it. Cut that number in half before adding anything to the roadmap.

carousel.title: Start from the question
carousel.body: Write the specific uncertainty you are resolving, not the feature you want to build. A vague question produces a build that cannot fail and therefore teaches nothing.

carousel.title: Build only the instrument
carousel.body: Include what is needed to get an answer and nothing else. Every extra piece adds time to the loop and makes it harder to attribute the result to any one thing.

carousel.title: Measure behaviour
carousel.body: Watch what people do rather than what they say. Stated intent is a poor predictor, so design the test so that the answer shows up in an action.

carousel.title: Decide in the open
carousel.body: Write the conclusion down and state whether you are continuing or changing direction. Undocumented results quietly become whatever the loudest person remembers.

sparks.hook: Any metric that only ever goes up is telling you nothing.
sparks.insight: Total registered users, cumulative downloads and total revenue all rise with time regardless of whether the product is improving, which makes them comforting and useless. What tells you something is comparing groups of customers who arrived at different times: does the batch that joined last month behave better than the batch from three months ago? If later groups behave the same as earlier ones, your product changes are not working, however impressive the headline totals look on a chart.
sparks.why: Cumulative numbers hide the direction of travel because they cannot decrease. Splitting by arrival date is one of the few analyses that will actually contradict a team that wants to keep going.
sparks.apply: Rebuild your main dashboard so every number is a rate or a comparison between customer groups, and delete every cumulative total from it.

sparks.hook: A change of direction is a result, not a confession of failure.
sparks.insight: When the evidence says the current approach is not working, the choice is to change one major element of the plan while keeping what you have learned, or to keep going. Both are legitimate, and the common failure is not choosing at all: teams drift, changing small things repeatedly while the central assumption stays untested. Deciding on a schedule rather than in a crisis makes it a normal act of management. It also means the decision is made while there is still money left to act on it.
sparks.why: The word has been stretched to cover any change of plan, which drains it of meaning. The useful version is specific: keep one part of the model, change another, and be able to say which.
sparks.apply: Put a recurring date in the calendar for a persevere-or-change meeting, and require the team to bring evidence rather than opinions to it.

carousel.title: Gather the evidence
carousel.body: Bring cohort data, not anecdotes. The question is whether later customers behave better than earlier ones, because that is what shows whether your work is landing.

carousel.title: Name what changes
carousel.body: Decide which single element moves: the customer, the problem, the channel, the pricing, the technology. Changing everything at once is a restart, not a change of direction.

carousel.title: Keep the learning
carousel.body: Write down what you now know to be true regardless of direction. The value of the last six months is in that list, and it is easily thrown away in a reset.

carousel.title: Set the next checkpoint
carousel.body: Agree the evidence and the date that would trigger the next decision. Without a fixed checkpoint, persevering becomes the default by inertia rather than by choice.

sparks.hook: Small batches feel slower and finish sooner.
sparks.insight: Working in large chunks feels efficient because you set up once and process everything at once. In practice it delays feedback, hides defects until late, and means a mistake made at the start contaminates the entire batch. Shrinking the batch size means work reaches the point of judgement quickly, errors surface while they are cheap, and the queue of half-finished work stops growing. It borrows directly from manufacturing, where the same counter-intuitive result has been demonstrated for decades.
sparks.why: The mechanism is that large batches push discovery of problems to the end, when the cost of fixing them is highest. Small batches trade a little setup overhead for much earlier information.
sparks.apply: Take your largest piece of unreleased work and split it into pieces you can put in front of a real user within a week each.

sparks.hook: Fix the fifth cause, not the first. The first one is never the problem.
sparks.insight: When something breaks, the immediate cause is usually technical and the real cause is usually organisational.
