Asking why repeatedly moves you from the symptom to a training gap, a missing check, a rushed release process. The discipline is to make a proportionate investment at each level rather than a heroic fix at the surface. Done badly this becomes a search for someone to blame, which is why it only works where the person closest to the failure is the one running the analysis.
sparks.why: Repeated questioning is a crude but effective way to get past the first satisfying explanation. Its weakness is assuming a single causal chain when real failures often have several.
sparks.apply: At your next incident review, ask why five times in a row and commit to one small fix at each level rather than a single large one at the end.

sparks.hook: Optimising a small idea very efficiently is still a small idea.
sparks.insight: The most serious objection is that constant testing pulls you towards local improvement. Each experiment measures a small change against the current state, so the method reliably improves what exists and rarely produces something genuinely new. Several prominent investors have made this argument: some of the largest companies of the last two decades were built by people who committed to a long, unpopular bet that no early experiment could have validated. The method is strong on avoiding waste and weak on generating ambition.
sparks.why: Incremental testing cannot evaluate a proposition whose value only appears at scale or after years of building. Knowing which type of bet you are making tells you whether this toolkit applies at all.
sparks.apply: Ask whether your idea's value would show up in a small test. If it would not, set a milestone and a budget instead of an experiment.

sparks.hook: Speed is worthless if you are pointed at the wrong customer.
sparks.insight: A fast loop applied to the wrong question just gets you to a wrong answer sooner. The choice of who you are serving and what problem you are solving sits above the method and is not itself an experimental output. Teams often iterate energetically for a year inside a market they picked casually, improving conversion on a page that should never have existed. Before optimising the cycle, spend real time on the judgement call about which market and which problem, because that choice bounds everything the loop can achieve.
sparks.why: Experimentation optimises within a frame it cannot choose. This is the most common practical failure of the method: excellent process running on an unexamined premise.
sparks.apply: Write one page justifying your choice of customer and problem, and have someone outside the team argue against it before you plan another sprint.

actions: Write the two assumptions your business cannot survive without, and design one cheap test for whichever you have the least evidence for.
Measure the number of days between forming a question and holding data on it, then halve that number before adding anything new to the roadmap.
Rebuild your main dashboard so that every figure is a rate or a comparison between customer groups, and remove every cumulative total.
Book a recurring persevere-or-change meeting and require the team to bring cohort evidence rather than opinions to it.
not_for_you_if: You are making a long-horizon bet whose value cannot appear in a small test, or you want depth on strategy rather than on process.

verification.notes: Published 2011 by Crown Business. The method has been widely criticised for encouraging incremental improvement over ambitious bets. All prose here is original.

title: Zero to One
subtitle: Notes on Startups, or How to Build the Future
author: Peter Thiel and Blake Masters
why_it_matters: It is the sharpest available argument against the received wisdom that competition is healthy for the firms in it, and the clearest statement of how venture investing actually works. Whether or not you accept it, it forces you to defend your position.

crux.headline: Competition is not a badge. It is a tax
crux.body: A business in a genuinely competitive market makes no lasting profit, because rivals will keep bidding away whatever surplus appears. The businesses worth building are the ones that do something nobody else can do, and that keep doing it long enough for the returns to accumulate. So the aim is not to be a better version of an existing company but to make something new, then own the small market it creates before expanding outward.

sparks.hook: Every happy company is different. Every miserable one has competitors.
sparks.insight: Businesses that make sustained profits are doing something nobody else can do, which means each of them is unusual in its own way. Businesses stuck in fierce competition all look alike, because competition forces them to converge on the same practices and the same prices. The argument runs against how competition is normally described in business culture, where rivalry is treated as evidence of a healthy market and of your own toughness. For consumers it often is healthy. For the firms inside it, it is mostly a transfer of value to the buyer.
sparks.why: Read it as a claim about where profit accumulates, not as a policy position. Economists agree competitive markets compress producer margins; the disagreement is whether that is a problem to be solved or the point of the system.
sparks.apply: Write down what your company does that no rival could do within two years. If nothing survives that test, you are competing rather than building.

sparks.hook: What important truth do very few people agree with you about?
sparks.insight: The most useful question to ask a founder, or yourself, is where your beliefs diverge from consensus in a way you could defend. It is hard because most contrarian answers are either wrong or merely unpopular rather than genuinely unrecognised. But valuable companies are built on something true that most people have not yet accepted, since anything obvious has already been done by somebody better resourced than you. If your idea is widely agreed to be good, the returns have been competed away before you start.
sparks.why: The test filters for asymmetry of information or judgement, which is what an edge actually is. Its failure mode is rewarding contrarianism for its own sake, which produces confident nonsense rather than insight.
sparks.apply: Write one belief you hold that most people in your field reject, plus the evidence you would show them. Then ask a smart sceptic to attack it.

sparks.hook: Being first is worth little. Being last is worth everything.
sparks.insight: Moving early is often mistaken for the source of advantage, but the early mover carries the cost of educating a market and is frequently overtaken. What actually matters is generating the majority of the cash flows in your market for years after the excitement has passed. That reframes the question from how quickly you can launch to whether the business will still be dominant in a decade. Most valuations are made of distant cash flows, so a business that fades in five years is worth far less than its early growth suggests.
sparks.why: The point is that value sits in duration rather than in timing. Testing durability is hard and speculative, but asking it early prevents you from mistaking a fast start for a lasting position.
sparks.apply: Ask what your business will look like in ten years and what would have to be true for you to still lead. Write the three biggest threats to that.

sparks.hook: Four things separate a durable business from a lucky one.
sparks.insight: A position that lasts usually rests on some combination of four things: technology so much better that copying is impractical rather than merely expensive, a product that improves as more people use it, a cost structure that gets better with scale rather than worse, and a brand that buyers trust enough to pay for. One of these alone is fragile. Several together are why some businesses hold their position for decades while apparently similar rivals with more funding never establish one at all.
sparks.why: These are recognisable in most durably profitable businesses, though the framing is an argument rather than a study. Brand in particular can be a consequence of dominance rather than a cause of it.
sparks.apply: Score your business honestly on all four. If you cannot claim two of them, decide which one you will build before you spend on growth.

carousel.title: Proprietary technology
carousel.body: Not slightly better, but so much better on a dimension buyers care about that matching it would take a rival years. Marginal improvements get copied within a release cycle.

carousel.title: Network effects
carousel.body: The product gets more valuable as more people use it. These are powerful once established and brutally hard to start, since the early product is worth little to the first users.

carousel.title: Economies of scale
carousel.body: Costs per unit fall as you grow, so size itself becomes a defence. Service businesses often lack this, which is why they rarely produce durable dominance.

carousel.title: Branding
carousel.body: A name buyers trust enough to choose without comparison shopping. Real only when it rests on a genuine product difference, otherwise it is marketing spend with a short half-life.

sparks.hook: Start with a market so small that people laugh at the ambition.
sparks.insight: The instinct is to describe a huge addressable market, because a big number makes a plan look exciting. In practice a large market means a fragmented one with entrenched competitors, and a small share of it is worth very little. It is far better to dominate a tiny, specific group of users completely, because that gives you real revenue, real feedback and a defensible base. Expansion then happens outward into adjacent groups from a position of strength rather than as a scramble for scraps.
sparks.why: Dominating a niche gives you pricing power and word of mouth inside a group that talks to itself. The risk is picking a niche with no adjacent markets to expand into, which produces a comfortable business that cannot grow.
sparks.apply: Define a group of users small enough that you could serve most of them personally, and write down what winning all of them would take.

sparks.hook: One investment returns more than the entire rest of the fund.
sparks.insight: Venture returns are not spread evenly. A very small number of investments produce almost all the gains, and the rest collectively return roughly nothing. That has consequences beyond investing. It means a fund should only make bets that could plausibly be the outlier, since a moderately successful company does not move the total. It also means a founder should think hard about which company to join and which project to pursue, because effort spread across many options mostly lands in the part of the distribution that returns nothing.
sparks.why: Extreme skew in venture outcomes is well documented across funds. Applying the same logic to careers is an extension rather than a finding, and it understates how much people learn from the bets that fail.
sparks.apply: List where your time went last quarter. If it was spread across five things, pick the one that could matter most and give it half your hours.

sparks.hook: If you cannot name your distribution channel, you do not have one.
sparks.insight: Technical people systematically undervalue selling, because good selling is invisible when done well and embarrassing when done badly. But a product does not spread on merit alone, and the cost of acquiring a customer has to be lower than what that customer is worth over their lifetime, or the business does not work at whatever scale you reach. The right method depends almost entirely on deal size: an enterprise contract needs a person, a mid-sized purchase needs a repeatable sales process, and a cheap product needs distribution that costs almost nothing per user.
sparks.why: The distinction is practical and easy to check. Most failures here come from applying a sales model suited to one price point to a product priced at a completely different one.
sparks.apply: Calculate what a customer is worth over their lifetime and what you spend to get one. If the ratio is under three, fix distribution before building more product.

carousel.title: Work out the deal size
carousel.body: Average revenue per customer decides everything else about how you sell. Write it down before choosing a channel, because the channel has to be cheaper than the deal.

carousel.title: Match the method
carousel.body: Large contracts justify a person and a long cycle. Mid-sized ones need a repeatable process. Small ones need marketing or word of mouth, since no human can be involved profitably.

carousel.title: Check the arithmetic
carousel.body: Compare lifetime value against acquisition cost. A gap that only works at hypothetical future scale is not a business model, it is an argument for more funding.

carousel.title: Own one channel first
carousel.body: One channel working reliably beats five that half work. Spreading effort across channels usually means none of them reaches the volume where the economics improve.

sparks.hook: The belief that everything worth finding has been found is the mistake.
sparks.insight: There is a widespread assumption that the easy discoveries are done and the remaining questions belong to large institutions with large budgets. That assumption is convenient because it excuses not looking. Yet plenty of valuable things are unpopular to investigate, socially awkward to raise, or simply outside the areas where credentialled attention is currently pointed. The practical version is not mysticism: pick a domain, examine what everyone assumes without checking, and look specifically at the places where the assumption has never been tested.
sparks.why: Areas that are unfashionable are systematically under-searched because attention follows funding and status. That is a real structural gap, though it is also where a great deal of genuinely worthless work sits.
sparks.apply: Pick one thing everyone in your field takes for granted and spend a week trying to verify it from primary sources rather than from repetition.

sparks.hook: A plan you believe in beats optimism with no plan behind it.
sparks.insight: You can be optimistic or pessimistic about the future, and separately you can have a specific plan or none. The combination that builds things is optimism with a definite plan: the belief that the future can be better and a concrete idea of how to make it so. The dominant modern posture is optimism without a plan, which shows up as diversification, endless optionality and keeping doors open. That posture is rational for an individual managing risk and terrible for anyone trying to build something specific.
sparks.why: The distinction is a useful lens rather than a tested claim. It does explain why institutions that hedge everything struggle to produce anything, and why concentrated conviction is required for large projects.
sparks.apply: Write the specific future you are working towards and the sequence of steps to it. If you cannot, you are keeping options open rather than building.

sparks.hook: This is an argument from an investor with a stake in the conclusion.
sparks.insight: Two caveats belong with the book. It is written by a venture investor whose returns depend on the small number of firms that escape competition, so the advice to seek dominance describes what is good for that portfolio as much as what is good for the world. And the evidence is illustrative rather than systematic: memorable examples selected after the fact, without any account of the many founders who followed the same advice and failed. The reasoning is worth engaging with. The confidence exceeds what it can support.
sparks.why: The strongest objection is that concentrated market power benefits owners and often harms buyers, which the book treats as a secondary concern. Read it as a sharp partial argument rather than a balanced account.
sparks.apply: For each claim you find persuasive, ask who benefits if you believe it, then look for one counter-example before acting on it.

actions: Write down what your company does that no competitor could replicate within two years, and be honest if the list comes out empty.
Define a group of users small enough that you could serve nearly all of them, then plan what taking that whole group would require.
Calculate customer lifetime value against acquisition cost, and fix distribution before adding features if the ratio is weak.
Take the argument you found most convincing and spend an hour looking for the strongest published objection to it.
not_for_you_if: You want systematic evidence rather than argument, or you are uncomfortable taking strategic advice framed around building market power.

verification.notes: Published 2014 by Crown Business, developed from Blake Masters's notes on a Stanford course taught by Thiel in 2012. The argument is polemical and its examples are chosen retrospectively. All prose here is original.

title: Crossing the Chasm
subtitle: Marketing and Selling High-Tech Products to Mainstream Customers
author: Geoffrey A. Moore
why_it_matters: It explained why promising technology companies stall right after their first burst of success, and gave them a specific remedy rather than a diagnosis. Three decades on it remains the standard reference for taking a new product from enthusiasts to a real market.

crux.headline: Early enthusiasm does not become mainstream demand
crux.body: The people who buy something new first do it because it is new, and they will tolerate rough edges to get an advantage. The mainstream buys for the opposite reason: to avoid risk and to keep working. Nothing carries you from one group to the other automatically. The way across is to abandon breadth, pick one narrow group with an urgent problem, and become the obvious complete answer for exactly them.

sparks.hook: Your first customers bought because it was new. Nobody else will.
sparks.insight: Early adopters are drawn to a product precisely because it is unproven, since being early is how they get an advantage over their peers. That makes their enthusiasm a poor signal for everyone who comes after. The pragmatic majority want the opposite: proof that other people like them already use it without incident. So the qualities that won your first wave, novelty and ambition, are the exact qualities that make the next wave hesitate. Growth stalls not because the product got worse but because the buyer changed.
sparks.why: The two groups have opposite risk preferences, which is why testimonials from enthusiasts do not persuade pragmatists. A pragmatist reads an enthusiast's endorsement as evidence the product is still experimental.
sparks.apply: Look at your last ten customers and mark which bought for advantage and which bought to avoid risk. The mix tells you which side of the gap you are on.

sparks.hook: The pragmatist's first question is who else already uses this.
sparks.insight: Mainstream buyers reduce risk by copying other people in their own situation. Not any customer, and not a famous logo from a different industry: someone recognisably like them, with the same constraints, who has already done this successfully. That makes references the currency of the whole transition. It also explains the trap of scattered early wins across many industries, which produces a list of customers where no single buyer can find anybody similar to themselves.
sparks.why: Reference-seeking is rational behaviour when a purchase carries career risk. The practical implication is that ten customers inside one industry are worth far more than fifty spread across ten.
sparks.apply: Count how many of your customers sit in one industry with one job title. If the largest cluster is under five, stop selling broadly and concentrate.

sparks.hook: Attack one narrow segment as if you had no other option.
sparks.insight: The way across is not gradual expansion but concentration. Pick one specific group with a problem urgent enough that they are already spending money or losing money on it, and aim everything at them: the product roadmap, the sales effort, the partners, the case studies. The segment should be small enough that you can plausibly become the standard choice within it, because a dominant position in a small pond generates the references and word of mouth that carry you into the next one.
sparks.why: The logic is that word of mouth travels inside communities, not between them. Dominating a small connected group creates compounding referrals, while spreading thin creates none at all.
sparks.apply: Name one segment, defined by industry and role, that you could plausibly dominate this year, and decline the next deal that falls outside it.

carousel.title: Find urgent pain
carousel.body: Look for a problem the segment is already losing money on. Convenience will not persuade a risk-averse buyer to adopt something unproven; only an expensive, visible problem will.

carousel.title: Make it small enough
carousel.body: Choose a group you could realistically become the default choice for within twelve months. If it is too large to dominate, it is too large to start with.

carousel.title: Check it is connected
carousel.body: The members must talk to each other through conferences, associations or shared suppliers. Referrals cannot travel through a group whose members never meet.

carousel.title: Say no to everything else
carousel.body: Turning away good deals outside the segment is the hardest part and the whole mechanism. Every exception dilutes the focus that makes dominance possible.

sparks.hook: Nobody buys your product. They buy the whole solution to their problem.
sparks.insight: What you sell is only part of what a customer needs to get the outcome they want. There is also the integration, the training, the data migration, the compatible hardware, the consultants who know how to run it. Enthusiasts will assemble that themselves and enjoy doing so. Mainstream buyers will not, and a gap anywhere in the chain stops the purchase entirely. So the job is to define everything required for a customer in your chosen segment to succeed, then supply or arrange all of it, whether or not you build it.
sparks.why: This reframes the roadmap from features to completeness. It also explains why narrowing the segment is essential, since assembling everything needed is only affordable for one group at a time.
sparks.apply: Write every step a customer must complete to get value from you. Circle the ones you do not currently supply and find a partner for the biggest.

sparks.hook: Buyers do not want to be first. They want to be seventh.
sparks.insight: The mainstream buyer's calculation is dominated by what happens if this goes wrong, because the personal cost of a failed project exceeds the personal reward of a successful one. Being early offers upside they do not particularly want and risk they very much do not. Understanding this changes how you sell: emphasising innovation makes things worse, while emphasising that this is now the normal choice among their peers makes things better. You are not selling excitement to this group. You are selling the absence of career risk.
sparks.why: The asymmetry between the punishment for a visible failure and the reward for a quiet success is real in most organisations, and it makes conservative buying behaviour perfectly rational.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your main sales page so the first thing a cautious buyer sees is who already uses it, not what is new about it.

sparks.hook: Position yourself against an alternative, not against a description.
sparks.insight: Buyers cannot evaluate something with no reference point, so a product described only in its own terms gets filed under interesting and then forgotten. Positioning works by naming the thing you replace and the specific way you differ from it. That means choosing a competitive alternative deliberately, which is uncomfortable because it appears to shrink your ambition. It does the opposite: it gives the buyer a budget line to take the money from and a comparison their colleagues will already understand.
sparks.why: Comparison is how people assign value, and if you do not choose the comparison the buyer will pick one for you, usually the least flattering available.
sparks.apply: Write one sentence naming what you replace and the single dimension on which you are clearly better, then test it on someone outside your company.

sparks.hook: You cannot cross this in stages. It is a jump or nothing.
sparks.insight: The temptation is to hedge: keep serving the early enthusiasts while gradually courting the mainstream, keep the broad market message while adding some segment-specific material. That produces a product that is not focused enough for anyone and a sales effort spread across incompatible buyers. The transition requires committing the company to one segment with enough resource that dominance is achievable, and accepting the revenue you lose in the meantime. Half a crossing lands you at the bottom of the gap with less money than you started with.
sparks.why: The all-or-nothing framing is the most criticised part of the argument, and in practice many companies do transition gradually. It holds best where the whole product requirement is heavy and resources are scarce.
sparks.apply: Decide what share of engineering and sales capacity goes to your chosen segment. If it is under seventy percent, you have not actually committed.

sparks.hook: The people who won your first customers may not be able to win the next ones.
sparks.insight: Selling to enthusiasts rewards technical depth, improvisation and comfort with an unfinished product. Selling to the mainstream rewards process, references and reassurance. These are different skills and often different people, and the shift is one of the more painful parts of the transition because it can mean changing a team that has just succeeded. The same applies to the product organisation, where the emphasis moves from adding capability to removing rough edges nobody had complained about because early users worked around them.
sparks.why: The change is structural rather than a question of effort. A team optimised for one kind of buyer will keep producing what that buyer wanted, because that is what their instincts and their incentives reward.
sparks.apply: Audit whether your sales conversations lead with capability or with reassurance. If the wrong one dominates, change the script before changing the team.

carousel.title: Change the pitch
carousel.body: Lead with the problem and the proof rather than with the technology. A pragmatist stops listening once a conversation becomes a description of how clever the system is.

carousel.title: Build the reference set
carousel.body: Treat every early win in your segment as an asset to be documented properly. A named customer with a number attached is worth more than a new feature.

carousel.title: Industrialise delivery
carousel.body: Replace bespoke implementations with a repeatable process. Mainstream buyers are paying for predictability, and heroic custom work cannot be sold twice.

carousel.title: Fix the boring gaps
carousel.body: Documentation, onboarding, support hours, billing. Early users tolerated all of it. The next group will abandon the purchase over any one of them.

sparks.hook: The adoption curve was borrowed, and the gap in it was the new part.
sparks.insight: The underlying model of how new things spread through a population came from earlier research on the diffusion of innovations, which described adopters ranging from the venturesome few to the reluctant last. The contribution here was to argue that the transition between two of those groups is not smooth but a genuine discontinuity, because the two groups buy for incompatible reasons. Knowing which part is borrowed and which is the argument helps you judge how much weight each deserves.
sparks.why: The diffusion research is decades of empirical work across many fields. The claim of a specific discontinuity is an interpretation built on top of it, supported by cases rather than by systematic testing.
sparks.apply: Before applying the model, check whether your buyers genuinely fall into groups with different motives, or whether they are one population buying for one reason.

sparks.hook: The model was built for expensive sales, and much software no longer sells that way.
sparks.insight: The book assumes a purchase decided by a committee, carrying career risk and requiring a salesperson. A great deal of software now enters organisations from the bottom: an individual signs up, uses it, and the company formalises it later. That route inverts several conclusions, since the individual user faces little risk and needs no references. The framework still applies where the purchase is large, regulated or disruptive to operations. Check which world you are in before adopting the remedy.
sparks.why: Adoption mechanics changed with cheap distribution and self-service pricing. The underlying insight about differing buyer motives survives; the specific prescription about beachheads and heavy whole products does not always.
sparks.apply: Ask whether one person can adopt your product without permission. If they can, invest in the individual user experience before building a segment strategy.

actions: Cluster your existing customers by industry and job title, and identify the largest group that could plausibly be dominated within a year.
Map every step a customer must complete before they get value from you, then find a partner to close the largest gap you do not fill yourself.
Rewrite your main sales message to lead with proof from similar buyers rather than with what is new about your technology.
Decide what share of engineering and sales capacity is committed to your chosen segment, and write down the deals you will now turn away.
not_for_you_if: You sell a low-cost self-service product that individuals adopt without approval, or you want quantitative evidence rather than a well-argued model.

verification.notes: First published 1991 by HarperBusiness, revised several times since. The adoption curve derives from earlier diffusion of innovations research; the discontinuity claim is the book's own argument. All prose here is original.

title: The Effective Executive
author: Peter F. Drucker
why_it_matters: It was the first serious treatment of how a person doing knowledge work should organise their own effort, written before anyone used that term casually. Almost everything later written about focus and prioritisation restates parts of it, usually less precisely.

crux.headline: Effectiveness is a set of habits anyone can learn
crux.body: It is not intelligence, imagination or knowledge, none of which reliably convert into results. It is a handful of practices: knowing where your time actually goes, aiming at contribution rather than effort, building on strengths instead of patching weaknesses, concentrating on the few things that matter, and making decisions properly rather than frequently. All five are learnable, and none of them are natural.

sparks.hook: Intelligent, imaginative and knowledgeable people are often startlingly ineffective.
sparks.insight: The correlation between raw ability and results is much weaker than anyone expects. Brilliant people frequently produce little, while apparently ordinary people working methodically produce a great deal. That is because effectiveness is a separate skill from capability: it is about converting knowledge into outcomes, which requires a specific set of practices nobody is born with. The encouraging conclusion is that if effectiveness were a talent, most organisations would be doomed, since talent is rare. Being a habit, it can be taught.
sparks.why: The claim rests on a lifetime of close observation rather than measurement, so treat it as an experienced argument. Its practical value is in shifting attention from who someone is to what they do.
sparks.apply: Pick one of the five practices you handle worst and work only on that for a month, rather than trying to improve generally.

sparks.hook: You do not know where your time goes. Nobody does, and everybody thinks they do.
sparks.insight: Memory of how you spent your week is unreliable and consistently flattering. The only fix is to record it as it happens for a few weeks and then look at the record, which almost always produces an unpleasant surprise: hours consumed by meetings that could have been an email, by work that belonged to someone else, by interruptions from a system that is badly designed. Only after the record exists can you eliminate anything, because before that you are cutting from a fiction.
sparks.why: The gap between recalled and recorded time use is well established. It is also self-serving in a predictable direction, since we remember the deep work and forget the fragments.
sparks.apply: Log what you actually do in fifteen-minute blocks for two weeks. Then find the three biggest activities that produced nothing and cut one entirely.

carousel.title: Record honestly
carousel.body: Write down what you did as you do it, not once the day is over. Reconstructed logs smooth out the fragmentation, which is the exact thing you are trying to see.

carousel.title: Cut the pointless
carousel.body: Ask which activities would go unnoticed if you stopped altogether. There are always several, and they usually survive because a predecessor started them and nobody reviewed it.

carousel.title: Hand over what others can do
carousel.body: Anything someone else could do adequately should be theirs. Doing it yourself because you are faster is a habit that guarantees you never do the work only you can do.

carousel.title: Consolidate what remains
carousel.body: Assemble the leftover time into blocks large enough for real thinking. Time spent in fragments produces nothing regardless of how many hours it adds up to.

sparks.hook: Ask what results are expected of you, not what work you are doing.
sparks.insight: Most people describe their job in terms of effort and authority: what they oversee, how hard they work, how many people report to them. That framing keeps attention inside the organisation, where none of the results are. The more useful question is what outcome outside your own department would be missing if you did nothing. Answering it usually changes priorities immediately, because much of what fills a week turns out to serve internal process rather than any result anybody outside would notice.
sparks.why: Focusing on contribution redirects effort towards outputs and forces communication with the people who consume your work, which is where most organisational failure actually happens.
sparks.apply: Write the single result your role should produce this quarter for someone outside your team, then cut one recurring meeting that does not serve it.

sparks.hook: Hire for what someone can do, not for the absence of weaknesses.
sparks.insight: Selecting for the fewest flaws produces mediocrity, because the person with no obvious weaknesses usually has no notable strength either. The productive approach is to ask what a person is genuinely exceptional at and whether that strength matters for the role, then design around the weaknesses rather than trying to fix them. The same applies upward: work out what your boss does well and feed them work in that form. And it applies to yourself, since your own weak areas are unlikely to become strengths at any age.
sparks.why: Strengths tend to be stable and hard to build, while weaknesses can often be managed structurally. The obvious limit is that some weaknesses, particularly of integrity, cannot be designed around at all.
sparks.apply: For each person you manage, write their one genuine strength and one task you could shift to them that uses it more directly.

sparks.hook: Do one thing at a time, and the second thing usually turns out to be unnecessary.
sparks.insight: The scarce resource is not time but concentrated attention, and the only reliable way to produce something significant is to give one thing your best hours until it is finished. Running several priorities in parallel means each gets fragments, and fragments are enough to keep a project alive but not enough to complete it. There is also a curious benefit to sequencing: by the time you finish the first thing, circumstances have often changed enough that the second no longer needs doing.
sparks.why: Task switching carries a real cost in both time and quality, and the effect is larger for complex work. The difficulty is organisational, since most workplaces are structured to hand you several priorities at once.
sparks.apply: Choose the single most important thing on your list and give it your first two hours every day this week before opening anything else.

sparks.hook: Postponing a task is often the same as deciding never to do it.
sparks.insight: Everyone has a list of things they intend to get to later. In practice later rarely arrives, and the honest move is to decide explicitly whether something is being abandoned rather than deferred. That converts a growing pile of quiet guilt into a short list of real commitments. The same logic applies to existing activities. Ask periodically whether you would start each one today knowing what you now know, and drop the ones where the answer is no rather than waiting for them to fail.
sparks.why: Abandoning things deliberately frees the resources that new work requires. Organisations are structurally bad at this because every activity has someone whose job depends on its continuation.
sparks.apply: Take your list of postponed items and formally cancel the bottom third today, telling anyone affected rather than letting them quietly expire.

sparks.hook: Make fewer decisions, and make each one at a higher level.
sparks.insight: Effective people are not rapid deciders. They make relatively few decisions, because they treat most situations as instances of a recurring pattern rather than as unique events. The work is in recognising which pattern applies and then establishing a rule or principle that settles every future case of that kind. Deciding the same thing repeatedly under slightly different circumstances is the mark of someone handling symptoms. One correct decision at the level of the general problem removes the need for a hundred at the level of the specific.
sparks.why: Treating a recurring problem as unique produces inconsistent handling and endless managerial load. The failure mode is the opposite error: forcing a genuinely novel situation into an existing rule.
sparks.apply: Find a decision you have made three times this quarter, write the rule you have been using, and publish it so others can decide without you.

sparks.hook: A decision everyone agrees with has not been examined yet.
sparks.insight: Unanimity in a meeting usually means nobody has done the work, not that the answer is obvious. A sound decision requires genuine alternatives, which means someone must construct the strongest case against the preferred option. That is not politeness or balance; it is the only way to test whether the reasoning survives contact with a competent objection. It also produces something useful for later: if the decision goes wrong, the team already understands the alternative rather than starting the analysis from scratch under pressure.
sparks.why: Deliberate disagreement counters the tendency of a group to converge on an early favourite. Assigning the opposing case to a specific person makes it a duty rather than an act of courage.
sparks.apply: At your next significant decision, assign one person to argue the strongest opposite case and refuse to decide until they have done it properly.

carousel.title: Insist on alternatives
carousel.body: A single proposal is not a decision, it is a request for approval. Require at least one genuine alternative that someone is prepared to defend seriously.

carousel.title: Assign the objection
carousel.body: Name the person responsible for the strongest case against. Making it a role removes the social cost of dissent and stops the loudest opinion carrying the room.

carousel.title: Define what it must achieve
carousel.body: Write the conditions the decision has to satisfy before you compare options. Without them, the comparison becomes a contest of confidence rather than of merit.

carousel.title: Turn it into work
carousel.body: A decision is not made until someone owns an action with a deadline. Until that exists, you have recorded an intention and nothing has changed.

sparks.hook: Until someone has a deadline, you have an opinion rather than a decision.
sparks.insight: Most decisions fail in the gap between agreement and action. The meeting ends with everybody nodding, and nothing changes because no name was attached to any step and no date was set. Converting a decision into work means specifying who does what by when, who must be told, and what they need to be able to do. It is unglamorous and it is where the majority of organisational effort leaks away, which is why the person who insists on it at the end of a meeting is worth more than the person with the best idea in it.
sparks.why: The mechanism is simple accountability. Unassigned actions have no owner to feel their absence, so they fail silently and are discovered only at the next review.
sparks.apply: End every meeting by reading out each action with a name and a date attached, and send that list before anyone leaves the room.

sparks.hook: Written in 1966, and the parts that dated are the ones about typing pools.
sparks.insight: The book has held up unusually well because it addressed a problem that has only grown: work whose quality cannot be observed by watching someone do it. What has aged are the surface details, including an assumption that executives are men and an organisational world of secretaries and memoranda. The substance survives because the core difficulty is unchanged. If your output is judgement rather than units produced, nobody else can tell whether your week was well spent, so managing your own attention is not optional.
sparks.why: The argument is observational rather than empirical, which is a genuine limitation. Its endurance comes from describing a structural feature of knowledge work rather than a management fashion of its decade.
sparks.apply: Ask whether anyone could tell from outside whether your week produced anything. If not, define your own measure of contribution and review it weekly.

actions: Log your time in fifteen-minute blocks for two weeks, then eliminate the largest activity that produced no result anyone outside your team would notice.
Write the single outcome your role should deliver this quarter for someone outside your department, and cancel one recurring commitment that does not serve it.
Find a decision you have made three times recently, write down the rule you have been applying, and publish it so others can decide without you.
Add a standing step to every meeting where each action is read out with an owner and a date before anyone is allowed to leave.
not_for_you_if: You want empirical research rather than distilled observation, or you need tactics for a specific job rather than general habits of working.

verification.notes: First published 1966 by Harper & Row. The argument rests on Drucker's consulting observation rather than on empirical study, and the surface examples reflect the corporate world of the 1960s. All prose here is original.

title: Management
subtitle: Tasks, Responsibilities, Practices
author: Peter F. Drucker
why_it_matters: It is the closest thing management has to a foundational text, assembling a scattered set of practices into a discipline with its own questions and responsibilities. Much of what business schools now teach as basic was first set out at length here.

crux.headline: A business exists to create a customer
crux.body: Profit is not the purpose of an enterprise but the test of whether it is working and the cost of staying in existence. The purpose sits outside the organisation, in someone who chooses to buy. That reversal drives everything else: only two functions actually produce results, which are marketing and innovation, and every other activity is a cost. It also makes the central question what the customer considers value, which is rarely what the company thinks it sells.

sparks.hook: Profit is not why a business exists. It is the cost of continuing to exist.
sparks.insight: Treating profit as the purpose gives you no guidance about what to actually do, and it misdescribes what profit is for. It covers the risks of being in business, funds the replacement of what wears out, and pays for whatever comes next. A business that fails to earn enough of it is destroying resources, so the requirement is real and non-negotiable. But the purpose lies outside the company, in creating someone willing to buy. Profit is how you know that purpose is being served, not the reason you were founded.
sparks.why: The distinction changes what you measure and what you optimise. A firm managed as if profit were the goal will reliably harvest its own future, since cutting investment always improves this year's number.
sparks.apply: Write what your business exists to do for someone outside it, then check whether your top three metrics measure that or only measure the money.

sparks.hook: The customer decides what your business is, and they rarely agree with you.
sparks.insight: Companies describe themselves by what they produce. Customers describe them by what problem gets solved, and the two descriptions can be startlingly different. A firm that thinks it sells equipment may in fact be selling uptime, and one that thinks it sells software may be selling the ability to fire a supplier. Since the customer's definition is the one that determines whether they buy, the useful exercise is to ask what they consider valuable and to accept the answer even when it makes your engineering achievements look irrelevant.
sparks.why: Getting the definition wrong misdirects investment for years, because the company keeps improving the thing it believes it sells rather than the thing being bought.
sparks.apply: Ask ten customers what they would lose if you disappeared tomorrow. If their answer differs from your product description, rewrite the description.

sparks.hook: Only two activities produce revenue. Everything else on the payroll is a cost.
sparks.insight: An enterprise gets results from finding out what people need and creating something that meets it, and from producing something genuinely new. Both point outward at the market. Every other function, however necessary, consumes resources rather than generating them. That is not an argument for cutting them, since a business without finance or operations collapses quickly. It is an argument for knowing which is which, because organisations drift towards spending their attention on internal activity, where the meetings are and where the politics are.
sparks.why: The framing is a useful corrective to internally focused management. It undersells the competitive advantage that operations can create, which several modern firms have built entire positions on.
sparks.apply: Count the hours your leadership team spent last month on internal matters versus on customers and new offerings, and rebalance the calendar.

sparks.hook: Answer what our business should be, not just what it is.
sparks.insight: Two questions have to be asked together and rarely are. What is our business, answered honestly from the customer's side, and what should it be given where the market and technology are going. Asking only the first produces a company that describes its present accurately and walks into the future backwards. Asking only the second produces fantasy strategy disconnected from what you currently do well. The pairing is uncomfortable because the honest answer often implies abandoning something profitable that everyone is fond of.
sparks.why: Most planning answers neither question and instead extrapolates last year. The value here is in forcing an explicit statement that can later be checked against what happened.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph on what your business is and one on what it should be in five years, then name the first thing that has to be given up.

carousel.title: Define it from outside
carousel.body: Describe the business in the customer's terms: what problem they hand to you and what they would do without you. Internal descriptions are almost always too flattering.

carousel.title: Ask what it should be
carousel.body: Given where technology, demographics and buying behaviour are heading, what should you be doing in five years? Write it as a description, not as a target number.

carousel.title: Ask what it should not be
carousel.body: Name the activities that will no longer belong. This is the question everyone skips, and it is the only one that releases the resources the new answer requires.

carousel.title: Set the abandonment date
carousel.body: Attach a real date to stopping one thing. Without a date, abandonment becomes something the organisation intends to do after the current busy period, which never ends.

sparks.hook: People manage themselves better when they set the targets they are judged on.
sparks.insight: The proposal was that each manager should work out what their unit must contribute to the wider goals, agree it upward, and then be measured against their own stated commitment. The self-control part is the point. Someone who has defined their own target and can see their own results does not need supervision to correct course, because they get the feedback directly. It replaces control from above with control by the person doing the work, which is the only kind that operates fast enough to matter.
sparks.why: The idea was widely distorted into cascading numeric quotas imposed from the top, which is close to the opposite of what was proposed and which quality thinkers criticised heavily for driving people to hit numbers by any available means.
sparks.apply: Ask each direct report to write what their team should be judged on next quarter, negotiate rather than dictate it, and give them the data to see it.

sparks.hook: Every decision is about the future, which is why none of them are safe.
sparks.insight: A manager decides now and finds out later, always with incomplete information and always about circumstances that have not happened yet. Waiting for certainty is not a cautious strategy but a decision to let events choose for you. What makes the risk manageable is being explicit about the time dimension: how long until this commitment pays back, how long until it can be reversed, what the world would have to look like for it to be right. Those questions turn a gamble into a bet with known terms.
sparks.why: Naming the time horizon prevents the common error of judging a long commitment by short-term results, which is how sound investments get cancelled halfway through.
sparks.apply: For your next significant commitment, write the payback horizon and the point at which you could still reverse it, and share both with your team.

sparks.hook: Structure follows strategy, and most reorganisations get the order backwards.
sparks.insight: Organisational design is not a matter of taste or of copying whoever is admired this year. It follows from what the business has decided to do and what activities are genuinely critical to that. Reorganising first and hoping strategy emerges from the new boxes is common and produces years of disruption for nothing. Where possible, the aim is units small enough to see their own results, with real responsibility for a market, because that is what allows people to manage themselves rather than waiting for instruction.
sparks.why: The sequence matters because structure encodes priorities. A reorganisation done without a strategy simply redistributes power and then forces the strategy to fit the new arrangement.
sparks.apply: Before your next reorganisation, write the strategy it serves on one page. If you cannot, postpone the reorganisation rather than the strategy.

sparks.hook: Treat people as a cost and you will get exactly the output a cost provides.
sparks.insight: The insistence was that the people doing the work are a resource capable of judgement and improvement rather than a variable expense to be minimised. That has practical consequences: the person closest to a process usually knows most about it, so their knowledge should be sought rather than overridden, and responsibility should sit as close to the work as possible. It was a genuinely unpopular position when much of industry still treated labour as interchangeable, and it anticipated most of what later became standard practice.
sparks.why: Later evidence on autonomy and on frontline knowledge broadly supports the direction. The counterweight is that responsibility without matching authority or information produces stress rather than performance.
sparks.apply: Ask the people closest to your worst process what they would change, then implement one of their suggestions without modifying it.

sparks.hook: Do the job well and something else will still deteriorate. Plan for it.
sparks.insight: Managing means holding several obligations that pull in different directions: the results this year, the capacity to produce results in ten years, and the effect of the enterprise on the society it operates in. None can be sacrificed indefinitely without the others failing, and no formula resolves the tension. The practical response is to keep all three visible in the same conversation, because whichever one is absent from the discussion is the one being quietly funded by the others.
sparks.why: Making the trade-offs explicit does not resolve them, but it prevents the most common failure, which is optimising the measurable short-term obligation because it is the only one on the dashboard.
sparks.apply: Add one long-horizon measure and one external-impact measure to your regular review, next to the financial ones, and discuss all three together.

carousel.title: Name the immediate result
carousel.body: What the enterprise must deliver in the current period to remain viable. This is the obligation that will always be represented, because it is the easiest to count.

carousel.title: Name the future capacity
carousel.body: What must be built now to still be in business in a decade: people, capability, research, relationships. It has no deadline, which is why it is the first thing cut.

carousel.title: Name the external effect
carousel.body: The consequences of your operations for the people and communities around them. Ignoring it invites regulation that will be shaped by people who dislike you.

carousel.title: Review the three together
carousel.body: Put all three in the same meeting with the same seriousness. Whichever is absent from the discussion is being financed silently by the other two.

sparks.hook: It is enormous, occasionally repetitive, and still the reference nobody replaced.
sparks.insight: Two honest caveats. It is a very long book written for a world of large, mostly national, mostly manufacturing corporations, and the examples reflect that. And its most famous proposal was widely implemented as a top-down numbers regime that produced the opposite of what was intended, which is a fair criticism of how the idea travels even if not of the idea itself. What survives is the framing: that management is a genuine discipline with obligations, not a set of techniques for extracting more work from people.
sparks.why: The reasoning is observational and synthetic rather than empirical, so specific prescriptions should be tested rather than adopted. The framing has outlasted almost every management fashion published since.
sparks.apply: Read one section rather than the whole book, starting with the chapters on what your business is, and apply the questions before reading further.

actions: Write one paragraph on what your business is from the customer's side and one on what it should be in five years, then name what has to be abandoned.
Ask ten customers what they would lose if you disappeared, and compare their answers against how your company describes itself.
Ask each direct report to propose what their team should be judged on next quarter, negotiate it rather than dictating it, and give them the data.
Add a long-horizon measure and an external-impact measure to your regular review so they are discussed alongside the financial numbers.
not_for_you_if: You want something short and practical, or you need guidance for a small modern company rather than a treatise on the large corporation.

verification.notes: First published 1973 by Harper & Row; a revised edition with Joseph A. Maciariello appeared in 2008. Management by objectives was widely implemented as top-down quota setting and criticised on that basis. All prose here is original.

title: Playing to Win
subtitle: How Strategy Really Works
author: A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin
why_it_matters: It turns strategy from a document into a set of five linked choices a team can actually argue about and answer. For anyone who has sat through a planning cycle that produced ambitions instead of decisions, it is the most useful practical guide available.

crux.headline: Strategy is choosing what not to do
crux.body: A strategy is an integrated set of choices that places you somewhere specific and gives you a way to win there. It is not a vision, a plan, a budget or a list of aspirations, because none of those require giving anything up. If your strategy does not name markets you will not enter and customers you will not serve, you have written a statement of intent that every competitor could also have signed.

sparks.hook: If your rival could sign your strategy document, it is not a strategy.
sparks.insight: Most strategy statements survive because nobody could object to them: serve customers well, grow profitably, be a great place to work. The test is whether a competitor could adopt the same words without changing anything they do. A real strategy contains choices somebody in the room disagreed with, and it names what you are giving up. Discomfort at the moment of writing is the signal you have got one, since a choice that costs nothing to make is not a choice, it is a description of your current position with adjectives attached.
sparks.why: The test is fast and hard to argue with. It exposes the common failure where a planning process produces goals and budgets while carefully avoiding any commitment that forecloses an option.
sparks.apply: Take your current strategy statement and cross out every sentence a competitor could also sign. Judge what is left on its own.

sparks.hook: Five questions, answered together, or you do not have a strategy.
sparks.insight: The framework is a cascade rather than a checklist, because the answers have to reinforce each other. What does winning actually mean for you. Where will you compete, specifically. How will you win there, in a way rivals cannot easily copy. What capabilities must exist for that to be true. And what systems will build and sustain those capabilities. Answering any one in isolation produces an orphan: a bold aspiration with no market attached, or a capability programme serving no particular way of winning.
sparks.why: The cascade forces consistency, which is where most strategy work fails. Firms routinely choose a premium position and then build management systems that reward volume.
sparks.apply: Answer all five questions on one page with your leadership team, then check each answer against the one above and below it for contradictions.

carousel.title: Define winning
carousel.body: State what winning means in concrete terms for your specific business and customers. Playing to participate is a legitimate choice, but make it consciously rather than by default.

carousel.title: Choose where to play
carousel.body: Name the segments, geographies, channels and categories you will compete in, and by omission the ones you will not. Everywhere is not an answer to this question.

carousel.title: Decide how to win
carousel.body: Say what will make customers choose you there rather than a rival. Broadly this means being structurally cheaper or being genuinely different, and you must pick.

carousel.title: Name the capabilities
carousel.body: List the few things you must be excellent at for that way of winning to hold, and be honest about which of them you do not currently have.

carousel.title: Build the systems
carousel.body: Decide what measures, structures and processes will create and sustain those capabilities. Without this step the strategy stays on the page and nothing changes.

sparks.hook: Most companies are playing to play and pretending otherwise.
sparks.insight: There is a real difference between organising to win and organising to keep participating respectably. Playing to participate looks like reasonable targets, incremental improvement and an unwillingness to take any position that could be wrong. It is often the rational choice, particularly in a declining market where the sensible move is to harvest. What is corrosive is doing it while claiming otherwise, because the language of ambition combined with the behaviour of caution demoralises everyone who takes the language seriously.
sparks.why: Naming which one you are doing changes what you should measure and how you should invest. A harvesting business managed as if it were growing wastes capital in both directions.
sparks.apply: Ask your leadership team whether the current plan is designed to win or to participate. Write down which, and align the targets to that answer.

sparks.hook: Where you compete matters more than how well you compete there.
sparks.insight: Choosing the field is the higher-leverage decision, and it is the one most companies inherit rather than make. That means naming the customers, geographies, channels and product categories where you will play, which necessarily means naming where you will not. The exclusions are the substance. A strategy that keeps every option open cannot concentrate resources anywhere, and concentration is the only way a smaller player ever beats a larger one on any part of the board.
sparks.why: Position determines the difficulty of everything downstream. A modest capability in a well-chosen segment beats an excellent one in a segment where a stronger rival is already entrenched.
sparks.apply: Write the three segments you will not serve this year, and tell the sales team so they can stop spending time qualifying them.

sparks.hook: Being generally good at things is not a way to win.
sparks.insight: How you win has to be specific enough that it explains why a customer chooses you over the alternative in front of them. Broadly there are two coherent answers: you are structurally cheaper to run so you can undercut and survive, or you are different in a way people will pay a premium for. Wanting both, without changing the operating model that would make both possible, results in an offer that is neither. The test is whether you can name what you deliberately do worse than your rivals in order to be better at the thing that matters.
sparks.why: Advantage requires a trade-off. If you cannot name what you are deliberately worse at, you have described an ambition to be excellent rather than a mechanism for winning.
sparks.apply: Write the one thing you are deliberately worse at than your competitors and why that choice makes you better at what customers actually buy on.

sparks.hook: A capability that works alone is one a competitor can buy.
sparks.insight: Strength comes from a handful of capabilities that reinforce each other, not from any single excellent function. A rival can hire your best people or copy one process, but reproducing a set of activities that only work in combination requires them to change several things at once, which is expensive and usually contradicts something they already do well. So the question is not which capability is strongest but how the pieces support each other, and whether removing one would degrade the rest.
sparks.why: Systems of mutually reinforcing activities are far harder to imitate than individual strengths, because copying one piece without the others produces cost with no benefit.
sparks.apply: Draw your top five capabilities and the links between them. If none of them depend on each other, expect your position to be copied within two years.

sparks.hook: Whatever you measure quietly overrules whatever you decided.
sparks.insight: The last stage of the cascade is the one that gets skipped, and it is where strategies die. If you have chosen a premium position but the sales team is compensated on volume, the compensation wins. If you have chosen speed but every decision needs four approvals, the approvals win. Management systems, measures and incentives are the mechanism by which a strategy becomes behaviour, and until they change, the strategy exists only in a document that people have read and then returned to their normal work.
sparks.why: Incentives and processes describe the organisation's real priorities more accurately than any statement of intent, because they operate every day without anyone having to remember them.
sparks.apply: List your team's three main incentives and check each against your stated strategy. Change the one that most clearly rewards the opposite behaviour.

sparks.hook: Stop asking what is true. Ask what would have to be true.
sparks.insight: Strategy debates stall because each side defends a position and attacks the others, so the discussion becomes about who is right rather than about what is uncertain. The productive reversal is to take each option seriously and ask what conditions would have to hold for it to be the best choice. That converts an argument into a list of testable statements, and it usually reveals that the disagreement rests on one or two beliefs about the market. Then you go and find evidence on those rather than continuing to argue.
sparks.why: It lowers the social cost of changing your mind, because nobody has to be wrong. People will help test a condition they proposed, while they will defend a position they have staked.
sparks.apply: For your biggest open decision, list what would have to be true for each option, then rank the conditions by how uncertain and how important each one is.

carousel.title: Lay out real options
carousel.body: Generate several genuine possibilities, including one nobody in the room likes. A single proposal with a straw alternative is not a choice, it is a request for approval.

carousel.title: Ask what must be true
carousel.body: For each option, write the conditions that would have to hold for it to be the best one. Frame them as statements about the world, not about who is right.

carousel.title: Find the shakiest condition
carousel.body: Rank the conditions by how confident you are and how much rests on them. The one that is both uncertain and load-bearing is the only one worth researching.

carousel.title: Test it, then choose
carousel.body: Design the cheapest evidence that would settle that condition, gather it, and let the result decide. Agree the decision rule before you see the data.

sparks.hook: Certainty is not available, so stop designing processes that assume it.
sparks.insight: Strategy is a bet about the future made with incomplete information, and the aim is to improve the odds rather than to eliminate doubt. Planning processes that demand a confident forecast for every option systematically favour the safest choice, because only the familiar option can be forecast credibly. That is how organisations end up choosing the least ambitious path while believing they were being rigorous. The honest posture is to name the uncertainty, state what you are betting on, and set the checkpoints where you will find out.
sparks.why: Demanding certainty biases decisions towards incrementalism, since novel options can never produce the same quality of forecast as an extension of what you already do.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your next proposal to state the bet, the odds you assign, and the date you will know. Remove any forecast you cannot honestly defend.

sparks.hook: It is written by a chief executive about his own record, and that shows.
sparks.insight: The framework is genuinely useful and the evidence for it is not what it appears. The cases come mostly from one large consumer goods company during the period one of the authors ran it, described afterwards by the person responsible. That is testimony, not a test, and it cannot show that the method produced the results rather than describing them well. Some of the celebrated moves also aged poorly, including a very large shaving acquisition that was later written down by billions, and a portfolio that was subsequently cut back sharply.
sparks.why: Retrospective accounts by successful leaders overstate how deliberate the successes were and understate the role of conditions. Use the questions, which are sound, and discount the case evidence.
sparks.apply: Run the five questions on your own business rather than studying the examples, and record your answers so you can check them against reality in a year.

actions: Answer all five cascade questions on a single page with your leadership team, and check each answer for contradictions with the ones above and below it.
Cross out every sentence in your current strategy that a competitor could also sign, then judge whether anything meaningful is left.
Write down the three segments you will not serve this year and tell the sales team so they stop spending time on them.
Audit your team's three main incentives against the stated strategy and change the one that most clearly rewards the opposite behaviour.
not_for_you_if: You want independent evidence rather than a retrospective account, or you need theory rather than a practical process for a leadership team.

verification.notes: Published 2013 by Harvard Business Review Press. The case material is drawn largely from Lafley's own tenure at Procter & Gamble and is retrospective rather than tested. All prose here is original.
